docs.title: PixelPro for ComfyUI
docs.text:
The retouching desk you already know (frequency separation, luminosity masks, LUTs, layer stacks, hair-accurate mattes, face alignment) rebuilt as 64 GPU nodes for ComfyUI.

Get started Browse the nodes GitHub

docs.title: Why PixelPro
docs.text:
• Real retouch techniques

    Not filters with fancy names. Frequency separation, luminosity masking, LAB colour matching, Laplacian-pyramid blending and closed-form matting work the way a retoucher expects.

  • GPU first, CPU safe

    Built on PyTorch and Kornia. Heavy filters run on CUDA and keep their memory bounded. The same nodes still run, slower, on a CPU-only machine.

  • Works with your AI pipeline

    Align a face, run your inpaint or ControlNet pass, paste it back seamlessly. Build masks for any upstream segmenter, and check results with SSIM/PSNR.

  • Tested and documented

    800+ automated tests, a sample workflow for every recent node, and this guide in English and Vietnamese.

docs.title: Explore by task
docs.text:
• Color & Tone

    ACR-style grading, tone curves, colour matching, LUT import/export and CLAHE local contrast.

  • Masks

    From a rough segmentation to a clean, hair-accurate alpha: refine, matte, clean up and preview.

  • Face

    Detect, map 468 landmarks, reshape, align and paste back, plus skin-tone masks.

  • Filters

    Frequency separation, edge-aware skin smoothing and halo-free sharpening.

  • Compositing

    A Photoshop-style layer stack with 27 blend modes, and seamless multi-band blending.

  • Geometry

    Face alignment, lens distortion correction and automatic alignment of a second shot.

  • Looks

    Finished colour looks from one dropdown, with an intensity control.

  • QA

    Measure what an edit changed: SSIM, PSNR, and a heatmap of where it changed.

docs.title: A typical portrait chain
docs.text:
Load Image
  → Face Detect Lite ──→ Facial Aligner ──→ (your AI or retouch pass) ──→ Unwrap Face
  → Frequency Separation / Skin Smoother  (skin)
  → Smart Sharpen + Detail Mask            (eyes, hair)
  → ColorLab or LUT Preset                 (colour)
  → QA Image Diff                          (check the result)

Each step is one node. Start with Quickstart, or open the examples.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text: Group Nodes Highlights Color & Tone 14 ColorLab (ACR-style), Tone Curve, Color Matcher (global and region), LUT Preset / Import / Export, HALD, Tone Match LUT, CLAHE Masks 11 Sub-Pixel and Edge-Aware refiners, Alpha Matte, Trimap, Morphology, Combine, Edge Smoother, Cleanup, Preview, Detail Mask Face 8 Face Detect (MediaPipe) and Detect Lite (YuNet GPU), 468 landmarks, Delaunay and TPS warp, Unwrap, Beauty Blend, skin-tone masks Compositing 5 Layer stack (start, add, group, flatten), Pyramid Blend Filters 5 Frequency Separation and Recombine, Skin Smoother, Smart Sharpen, Dust & Spot Removal Depth 2 Depth Anything V2, Depth Lens Blur (bokeh) Geometry 3 Facial Aligner, Lens Distortion, Auto Align Looks 1 Look Select QA 1 QA Image Diff Total 50 v1.5.x · Apache-2.0

docs.title: Quickstart
docs.text: Five minutes from install to your first result.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
ComfyUI Manager (recommended)Manual (git)
  1. Open Manager → Custom Nodes Manager.
  2. Search for ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro and click Install.
  3. Restart ComfyUI.
cd ComfyUI/custom_nodes
git clone https://github.com/jetthuangai/ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro.git
cd ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro
pip install -r requirements.txt

Use the same Python that runs ComfyUI (for a portable or venv install, its own python). Then restart ComfyUI.

Requirements

Python 3.10+, the PyTorch that comes with ComfyUI, Kornia ≥ 0.7, MediaPipe ≥ 0.10, OpenCV ≥ 4.8 and SciPy ≥ 1.10. Optional: onnxruntime-gpu (or onnxruntime) for Depth Anything and Depth Lens Blur. An NVIDIA GPU with 8 GB VRAM or more is recommended. Everything also runs on CPU, just slower.

docs.title: 2. Find the nodes
docs.text:
Right-click the canvas (or double-click and search), then open Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro. Nodes are grouped the same way as this site:

color · mask · face · compositing · filters · geometry · looks · qa

Tip

Type part of a node name in the search box, for example Frequency, Matte or CLAHE.

docs.title: 3. Run your first workflow
docs.text:
1. Copy workflows/sample_portrait.jpg from the pack folder into ComfyUI/input/.
  2. Drag a sample workflow onto the canvas. Good first picks:
    • CLAHE Local Contrast example: one node, instant result.
    • Face Detect Lite example: face box, landmarks and alignment.
    • Mask Cleanup example: also copy workflows/sample_binary_mask.png into ComfyUI/input/.
  3. Press Queue Prompt. Change one setting at a time and compare.

All sample workflows are listed in Examples.

docs.title: 4. Build your own chain
docs.text:
A good way to learn the pack is one classic retouch step per group:

Goal Try Even out skin but keep pores Frequency Separation or Skin Smoother Sharpen eyes and hair only Detail Mask → Smart Sharpen Grade colour like Camera Raw ColorLab, Tone Curve Match one photo to another Color Matcher or Color Matcher Region Cut out hair cleanly Trimap Builder → Alpha Matte Run AI on a face, paste it back Face Detect Lite → Facial Aligner → … → Unwrap Face Check what changed QA Image Diff

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
The nodes do not show up

Check the ComfyUI console for an import error from ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro. Usually a dependency is missing: run pip install -r requirements.txt with ComfyUI's own Python, then restart.

Face Detect Lite or Auto Align (LoFTR) downloads something

Yes, on first use only. Face Detect Lite downloads its YuNet weights (about 0.4 MB) and Auto Align with method = loftr downloads LoFTR weights (about 45 MB) into the torch cache. Face Detect (MediaPipe) downloads its model (about 5 MB) into ComfyUI/models/mediapipe.

The machine slows down on a big image

Turn on tile_mode in Skin Smoother for anything larger than a preview. Since v1.5.2 tiles are sized to keep memory near 2 GB. Close other heavy workflows if VRAM is already full.

I changed the pack but nothing changed in ComfyUI

ComfyUI loads custom-node code once at start-up. Restart ComfyUI after updating the pack.

docs.title: Color & Tone
docs.text:
These nodes handle everything about colour and brightness: matching one image to another, shaping contrast with curves, grading with a Camera Raw style panel, selecting by tone or colour, and saving or applying LUTs. Use them to finish a retouch, to bring AI output back to a reference photo, or to build a repeatable look.

  • Color Matcher

    Pull the colours of one image toward a reference in LAB space.

  • Color Matcher Region

    Match one masked region to another, even across different image sizes.

  • ColorLab

    Camera Raw style Basic, HSL, Color Grading and Gray Mix in one node.

  • Shadows/Highlights Pro

    Lift shadows and recover highlights without halos, Camera Raw or Photoshop style.

  • Defringe

    Removes purple and green fringes along high-contrast edges, and lateral CA.

  • HDR Merge (bracket)

    Fuses bracketed exposures into one image with detail in shadows and sky.

  • Auto: Tone & White Balance

    One click: exposure, Whites/Blacks, Highlights/Shadows and colour cast, with the settings as a ColorLab preset.

  • Apply ColorLab Preset

    Put a ColorLab look on any photo or batch, with strength and mask.

  • Lightroom Preset (XMP)

    Your Lightroom / Camera Raw presets with a thumbnail browser and a report.

  • Lightroom Preset Contact Sheet

    Compare a whole preset collection on one photo.

  • CLAHE Local Contrast

    Adaptive local contrast on lightness only; colours stay intact.

  • Tone Curve

    Eight-point curves for contrast and colour balance, with presets.

  • Hue/Saturation per Range

    Shift hue or saturation inside one chosen colour band.

  • Luminosity Masking

    Soft shadow, midtone and highlight masks from image brightness.

  • Saturation Mask

    Mask the pixels whose colour strength falls inside a range.

  • LUT Preset

    Apply a bundled colour look from a dropdown with an intensity slider.

  • LUT Import

    Load any .cube LUT and apply it, with strength and optional mask.

  • LUT Export

    Save a graded chart as a portable .cube LUT.

  • HALD Identity

    Generate the neutral colour chart you grade and bake into a LUT.

  • Tone Match LUT

    Build a LUT automatically from the colour and tone of a reference image.

  • Palette Extract

    Pull the 2–16 dominant colours as swatches and HEX codes, plus a flat-colour (posterised) version.

docs.title: Typical chains
docs.text:
• Match and finish: Load Image → Color Matcher → Tone Curve → ColorLab → Preview Image
  • Grade only the shadows: Load Image → Luminosity Masking → use mask_shadows as the mask of Tone Curve or Hue/Saturation per Range
  • Bake a look into a LUT: HALD Identity → Tone Curve / ColorLab → LUT Export, then reuse it with LUT Import

docs.title: Compositing
docs.text:
These nodes turn ComfyUI into a Photoshop-style layer stack: a background, layers on top with blend modes, opacity, fill, masks and clipping, groups, and a final flatten. They are meant for deterministic finishing passes after generation or retouching, where you want to adjust one layer without redoing the rest. Pyramid Blend is the odd one out: it joins two images through a mask so the seam disappears.

  • Layer Stack Start

    Makes the background layer of a stack from an image.

  • Layer Add

    Adds a layer with blend mode, opacity, fill, mask and clipping.

  • Layer Group

    Merges a sub-stack into one layer, like a Photoshop group.

  • Layer Flatten

    Renders the stack back into a normal image.

  • Pyramid Blend

    Seamless two-image composite through a mask using multi-band blending.

docs.title: Typical chains
docs.text:
• Colour grade as layers: Load Image → Layer Stack Start → Layer Add (soft_light) → Layer Add (screen) → Layer Flatten → Preview Image
  • A look as one group: two Layer Stack Start chains → Layer Group (overlay, opacity 0.8) → Layer Flatten
  • Paste a retouched face back: LUT Preset on the face → Pyramid Blend through a face mask → Preview Image

docs.title: Depth
docs.text:
Depth nodes estimate how far every pixel is from the camera and use that map like a photographer uses a lens: to put the background (or foreground) out of focus after the shot.

  • Depth Anything V2

    Estimate a depth map from a single photo (near = white). Small model is Apache-2.0; Base/Large are non-commercial.

  • Depth Lens Blur

    Bokeh from depth: choose the focus plane (or let a face/subject mask pick it) and the depth of field.

docs.title: Typical chains
docs.text:
• Portrait background blur: Load Image → Face Detect Lite (face_mask) → Depth Lens Blur with the face mask as focus_mask. Depth is estimated inside the node.
  • Product shot: SAM One-Click Mask on the product → focus_mask of Depth Lens Blur.
  • Reuse the depth map: Depth Anything V2 once → its depth into several Lens Blur variants, or into Mask Preview to inspect it.

docs.title: Face
docs.text:
The face group covers everything a portrait retouch needs around the face itself: finding it, reshaping it, pasting an edited version back, and splitting skin into tone ranges. Most chains follow one pattern, described below, so you can send a small, upright face crop to an AI or retouch pass and return it to the full photo without touching the rest of the image.

  • Face Detect

    Finds faces with MediaPipe and returns five key points per face.

  • Face Detect Lite

    Fast YuNet detector with five key points, real confidence and a face mask.

  • Face Landmarks

    A dense 468-point map of the face, with a preview overlay.

  • Face Warp

    Reshapes the face triangle by triangle, strictly inside the face mesh.

  • Face Warp TPS

    Reshapes the face with one smooth field, no triangle seams.

  • Unwrap Face

    Pastes an edited, straightened face crop back into the original photo.

  • Face Beauty Blend

    Blends a retouched picture over the original through a mask and strength.

  • Skin Tone Tri-Region

    Splits skin into shadow, midtone and highlight masks.

  • Auto Blemish

    Finds faces and heals pimples and small marks, keeping skin texture.

docs.title: The align → edit → paste-back pipeline
docs.text:
AI skin passes, face restoration and detail enhancers work best on a small, upright face. The standard chain gives them exactly that and then puts the result back:

  1. Detect. Face Detect or Face Detect Lite finds the face and outputs five landmarks as landmarks_json.
  2. Align. Facial Aligner (in the Geometry group) turns the face into a straight, square crop (image_aligned) and also outputs inverse_matrix_json, the recipe for undoing the move.
  3. Edit. Run your AI or retouch pass on the aligned crop.
  4. Paste back. Unwrap Face takes the edited crop, the original photo and inverse_matrix_json, and returns the full photo with only the face area changed.
  5. Polish (optional). Face Beauty Blend mixes the result over the original through a mask, with a strength slider, so the retouch looks natural.

Keep the original image wired to both Unwrap Face and Face Beauty Blend. The untouched pixels outside the face come from there.

docs.title: Which node should I pick?
docs.text:
MediaPipe Face Detect or YuNet Face Detect Lite?

Choose When Face Detect Lite You want speed (batches, previews), a face mask, a real confidence score, or you do not have MediaPipe installed. It uses the GPU when available. Face Detect You already use MediaPipe, you want its eye-corner points, or you also run Face Landmarks and want both to agree.

Both give the same five-point output, and both work with the aligner. Neither feeds the warp nodes directly: those need the 468-point output of Face Landmarks.

Delaunay Face Warp or TPS Face Warp?

Choose When Face Warp TPS You want gentle, natural reshaping (slimming, eye or jaw tweaks) with no triangle seams, GPU speed, or you are matching landmarks from another photo (it has a smoothness control for detector noise). Face Warp The change must stay strictly inside the face mesh, or you want every one of the 468 points honoured locally. It runs on the CPU.

docs.title: Typical chains
docs.text:
• AI skin pass, pasted back: Load Image → Face Detect Lite → Facial Aligner → your AI pass → Unwrap Face → Face Beauty Blend.
  • Subtle reshaping: Load Image → Face Landmarks (source) and a second Face Landmarks (target) → Face Warp TPS → Preview Image.
  • Tone-targeted retouch: Load Image + skin mask → Skin Tone Tri-Region → one mask into Face Beauty Blend. See the Skin Tone Retouch example.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
Filters work on the picture itself: texture, edges and smoothness. Split detail from tone with frequency separation, soften skin without losing edges, and sharpen at the end. Together they cover the core of a portrait retouch.

  • Frequency Separation

    Splits an image into a smooth colour layer and a fine-detail layer.

  • Frequency Recombine

    Puts the low and high layers back together, with a slider to boost or soften texture.

  • Skin Smoother

    Smooths skin with an edge-preserving blur, with optional mask and tiled processing.

  • Smart Sharpen

    Unsharp mask with a noise threshold, luminance-only mode and a mask.

  • Dust & Spot Removal

    Find and heal small dark or bright specks (sensor dust, tiny blemishes), leaving larger shapes alone.

  • Heal / Content-Aware Fill

    Paint what should go; it is rebuilt from the rest of the photo.

  • Motion / Zoom Blur

    Motion blur along an angle, or a zoom burst toward a point, with a mask.

docs.title: Typical chains
docs.text:
• Natural skin: Load Image → Skin Smoother (strength 0.3 to 0.5, with a skin mask) → Smart Sharpen → Preview Image
  • Fix colour, keep pores: Load Image → Frequency Separation → edit low only → Frequency Recombine
  • Sharpen only the detail: Detail Mask → mask of Smart Sharpen

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
Geometry nodes fix the shape and position of the picture before you start retouching: straighten lens distortion, line up two shots, or bring a face into a standard upright frame. Doing this first keeps later edits predictable.

  • Facial Aligner

    Rotates, scales and crops a face to a standard square from five landmarks.

  • Lens Distortion

    Corrects (or adds) barrel and pincushion distortion with lens presets.

  • Auto Align

    Matches features between two photos and warps one onto the other.

  • Auto: Upright

    Levels the horizon and makes converging building lines parallel.

docs.title: Typical chains
docs.text:
• One-click base edit: Load Image → Auto: Upright → Auto: Tone & White Balance → params_json → ColorLab to fine-tune
  • Wide-angle portrait to face edit: Load Image → Lens Distortion → Face Detect Lite → Facial Aligner → edit → Unwrap Face
  • Match two shots: Auto Align → Color Matcher → Layer Add

docs.title: Looks
docs.text:
Looks are finished creative grades you can audition in one step. Instead of building a long colour chain, you pick a style from a dropdown, set how strong it is, and compare. This is the fastest way to find a direction before you refine it with the colour tools.

  • Look Select

    Six ready-made looks (teal and orange, golden hour, faded film and more) with an intensity slider and optional skin protection.

For .cube LUT based looks see LUT Preset, LUT Import and Tone Match LUT in the colour group.

docs.title: Typical chains
docs.text:
• Quick audition: Load Image → Look Select → Preview Image
  • Look with fine control: Look Select → Tone Curve → Preview Image
  • Copy a reference's feel: Tone Match LUT → LUT Import on your photo
  • Build and save your own look: HALD Identity → colour nodes → LUT Export

docs.title: Masks
docs.text: Masks decide where an edit happens: which pixels get smoothed, graded, replaced or cut out. This group covers the whole life of a mask, from cleaning up a rough AI selection, to softening and tightening its edge, to extracting a hair-quality cutout, to checking the result.

docs.title: Mask basics in plain language
docs.text:
• Binary mask: each pixel is either fully selected (1) or not at all (0). Fast and simple, but edges look hard and cut-out.
  • Soft mask / alpha matte: pixels along the edge hold in-between values, such as 0.5 for a pixel that is half subject, half background. This is what makes hair and fur blend into a new background.
  • Feather: a controlled soft transition across the edge. It hides the seam, but a plain blur can also eat into the subject.
  • Trimap: a hint map with three values, 0 = sure background, 0.5 = unknown, 1 = sure subject. Matting only has to solve the grey band, which is why hair edges come out so much better than with a simple threshold.
  • Closed-form matting: a method that solves the whole soft alpha at once, using the photo's own colours as a guide. It powers Alpha Matte.
  • Guide image: the original photo, given to a mask node so the edge can follow real boundaries in the picture.

docs.title: Pick the right mask tool
docs.text:
Your problem Use this node The mask has small floating specks or tiny holes Mask Cleanup The edge is hard and looks like a sticker Sub-Pixel Mask Refiner The edge is jagged or wobbly but the shape is right Mask Edge Smoother The mask edge sits a few pixels off the real subject edge Edge-Aware Mask Refiner Hair, fur or glass needs real transparency Trimap Builder, then Alpha Matte The mask is too big or too small by a few pixels Mask Morphology (dilate or erode) You need only an outline band around the edge Mask Morphology (gradient) You want to add, subtract or overlap two masks Mask Combine You want a mask of only the sharp, textured areas Detail Mask You want a mask of shadows, midtones or highlights Luminosity Masking You want to see what the mask actually covers Mask Preview You want to measure how much an edit changed the image QA Image Diff

  • Mask Cleanup

    Removes specks, fills small holes and feathers by distance.

  • Sub-Pixel Mask Refiner

    Turns a hard mask into a feathered one that stays solid inside.

  • Edge-Aware Mask Refiner

    Snaps the mask edge onto the real edges of your photo.

  • Mask Edge Smoother

    Smooths jagged edges with a bilateral filter, optionally photo-guided.

  • Trimap Builder

    Makes the sure-subject, unknown and sure-background map for matting.

  • Alpha Matte

    Hair-quality soft alpha from a trimap and the photo.

  • Decontaminate Colors

    Removes green-screen or sky colour from a cut-out's soft edges.

  • Sky Mask

    Soft mask of the sky without an AI model.

  • Mask Morphology

    Grows, shrinks, closes or outlines a mask.

  • Mask Combine

    Adds, subtracts, intersects or multiplies two masks.

  • Detail Mask

    Selects the sharp, detailed parts of a photo.

  • Mask Preview

    Shows a mask as an overlay, heatmap, black-and-white view or cutout.

  • SAM One-Click Mask

    Segment Anything: one point, a face box or a rough mask gives a clean object mask.

docs.title: Typical chains
docs.text:
• Clean AI cutout (product or portrait): Mask Cleanup → Edge-Aware Mask Refiner → Sub-Pixel Mask Refiner → Mask Preview
  • Hair-quality cutout: rough mask → Mask Cleanup → Trimap Builder → Alpha Matte (with the photo as guide) → Mask Preview in cutout mode
  • Edit only the textured areas: Detail Mask → Mask Combine with a subject mask (intersect) → use as the gate for your sharpen or smooth step

docs.title: QA
docs.text:
QA nodes measure a result instead of changing it. Add them at the end of a retouch chain to see how much an edit moved the image, to confirm that a change stayed inside the area you masked, or to compare two settings on the same input.

  • QA Image Diff

    Compares two images with SSIM, PSNR and MAE and draws a heatmap, absolute or SSIM-map difference.

  • Cull Score

    Ranks a batch by sharpness, exposure, closed eyes and duplicates; keeps the best.

For checking a mask rather than an image, use Mask Preview from the Masks group.

docs.title: Typical chains
docs.text:
• Did my retouch only change the skin? original and retouched image → QA Image Diff (add the skin mask to limit the numbers to that area) → read the changed_pct and the heatmap.
  • Compare two settings: run the same photo through two versions of a node → feed both results to QA Image Diff in ssim_map mode to see where the structure differs.
  • Check a smoothing pass: Skin Smoother → QA Image Diff against the original, then use Mask Preview on your skin mask to confirm they line up.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Short, practical ways into the pack. Each page or workflow gives a concrete chain you can load, run and then adapt to your own photos.

docs.title: Example pages
docs.text:
• LUT Preset Gallery: before/after comparisons for all six bundled LUT presets.
  • Skin Tone Retouch Chain: splitting a portrait into shadow, midtone and highlight masks for targeted retouching.

docs.title: Sample workflows
docs.text:
The full catalogue, with a description of each graph and the image credits, is in the workflows README. Some good places to start:

  • Frequency Separation and Recombine
  • Skin Smoother
  • Layer compositing: 5-layer cinematic grade
  • LUT Preset
  • Skin Tone Tri-Region (needs the external A Person Mask Generator pack)
  • Pyramid Blend

docs.title: How to run a sample workflow
docs.text:
1. Copy workflows/sample_portrait.jpg from the repository into ComfyUI/input/. The Load Image node only looks in that folder. The mask workflows also need workflows/sample_binary_mask.png there.
  2. In ComfyUI, open the Load menu and pick the workflow .json file, or drag it onto the canvas.
  3. Press Queue Prompt.

docs.title: Recommended first path
docs.text:
1. Start with the Quickstart.
  2. Run the LUT Preset workflow once to confirm that image input and output are wired correctly.
  3. Move to the Skin Tone Tri-Region workflow if your work is portrait retouching. It needs the external A Person Mask Generator pack; most other sample workflows use only core ComfyUI nodes and PixelPro.
  4. Try the layer compositing workflows when you want a repeatable finishing grade.

docs.title: LUT Preset Gallery
docs.text: LUT Preset ships six bundled generic Adobe Cube looks. The gallery below was generated from workflows/sample_portrait.jpg by running the actual node and saving before and after previews.

docs.title: What each preset is for
docs.text: Preset Use when neutral-identity You want to check your wiring or compare against a no-change baseline. warm-portrait You want a warmer, softer portrait direction without building a full grade. cool-portrait You want a cleaner, cooler cast for editorial or product-style portraits. cinematic-teal-orange You want a stronger split-tone look with cooler shadows and warmer skin-adjacent tones. soft-pastel You want lower-contrast, lighter colour for gentle beauty or social previews. high-contrast You want punchier separation for quick review images or a stronger starting grade.

docs.title: Try it yourself
docs.text:
Open the LUT Preset example workflow, choose your image in Load Image, and switch the preset dropdown. Lower intensity below 1.0 when the full LUT is too strong.

Want a look that is not on this list? Build one with HALD Identity and LUT Export, then apply it with LUT Import.

docs.title: Skin Tone Retouch
docs.text: Skin rarely needs one fix everywhere. This example shows how to build three tone masks from a portrait with Skin Tone Tri-Region, then use them to treat shine, mid skin tone and shadows separately.

docs.title: The chain
docs.text:
Load Image ──────────────────────────────┐
                                         ▼
Person / skin mask (optional) ──► Skin Tone Tri-Region
                                     ├─ shadow_mask
                                     ├─ midtone_mask
                                     └─ highlight_mask

The skin mask can come from any segmentation node. The sample workflow uses the person-mask node from the external A Person Mask Generator pack, which you need to install separately. Without a skin mask the whole frame is split by brightness, including hair, clothing and background.

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
1. Download the sample workflow and drag it onto the ComfyUI canvas.
  2. Copy workflows/sample_portrait.jpg into ComfyUI/input/ and pick it in Load Image.
  3. Run it and look at the three mask previews. White is where each range applies.

docs.title: Using the three masks
docs.text:
• highlight_mask: soften shine, or pull highlight colour back. Route it into a colour adjustment, or into Face Beauty Blend with a smoothed version of the image.
  • midtone_mask: the main skin-tone grade. Match colour to a reference with Color Matcher Region, or apply a LUT through Face Beauty Blend.
  • shadow_mask: lift or warm the shadows, or limit noise reduction to dark areas.

The three masks always add up to your skin mask, so edits made through them never overlap or leave gaps.

docs.title: Settings to try first
docs.text:
Setting Default When to change it shadow_cutoff 0.33 Lower it if the shadow mask grabs too much of the face. highlight_cutoff 0.66 Raise it to target only the brightest shine. soft_sigma 1.0 Raise it for softer transitions between ranges.

For every setting in detail, see Skin Tone Tri-Region. To check a mask before using it, add Mask Preview.

docs.title: Alpha Matte
docs.text:
The high-quality cutout node. Give it a photo and a three-zone map (sure subject, sure background, unsure edge) and it works out how transparent each unsure pixel is, which is what hair, fur and glass edges need.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → mask → Mask: Alpha Matte Good for Hair and fur cutouts, semi-transparent edges, clean subject extraction for compositing

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Three terms help here.

  • Binary mask: every pixel is fully in or fully out. Hair becomes a hard, chopped shape.
  • Soft alpha (matte): every pixel has a value from 0 to 1 saying how much of the subject it holds. A strand of hair that covers half a pixel gets about 0.5, so it blends naturally into a new background.
  • Trimap: a hint map with three values: 0.0 = definitely background, 0.5 = unknown, 1.0 = definitely subject. You only ask the algorithm to solve the unknown band, which keeps it accurate. Make one with Trimap Builder.

This node uses closed-form matting (Levin, Lischinski and Weiss, 2008). "Closed-form" means it solves for the whole alpha at once with maths, instead of guessing pixel by pixel. It assumes that inside a small window the photo colours lie roughly along a line between the subject colour and the background colour. That lets it tell a thin strand of hair from background clutter, using the photo itself as a guide.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Make a rough subject mask (SAM, rembg or a hand-painted mask).
  2. Connect it to Trimap Builder. Widen the unknown band so it fully covers the hair.
  3. Connect the trimap to trimap and the original photo to guide.
  4. Leave the other settings at their defaults. Preview alpha with Mask Preview in cutout mode.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip epsilon 1e-7 Numerical safety term for the local colour model. Range 1e-8 to 0.01. Leave at the default unless the result looks noisy. window_radius 1 Size of the neighbourhood used to model colours. 1 to 3. Raise it for blurry or low-contrast images. lambda_constraint 100.0 How strictly the result must respect the sure-subject and sure-background areas of the trimap. 1 to 10000. Higher keeps known areas locked. compute_device auto auto uses the GPU when the guide image is already on the GPU. cuda forces the GPU and errors if none is available. cpu forces the CPU. Leave on auto.

Output: alpha (MASK), soft values from 0 to 1.

Trimap format

The trimap must use only 0.0, 0.5 and 1.0 (a tolerance of 0.05 is allowed). Any other value raises an error. A hand-painted or blurred mask will not pass, so build it with Trimap Builder.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• The unknown band must cover all the fine detail. If hair strands fall in the "sure subject" zone, they stay solid. If background falls in the "sure subject" zone, it stays in.
  • Keep the unknown band as narrow as the detail allows. A narrower band gives a cleaner result.
  • Matting needs a colour difference between hair and background. Dark hair on a dark background is hard for any matting method.
  • Use colour decontamination or edge colour fixing in your composite to remove background colour from hair edges.
  • Work on a cropped region for very large images. This node solves a large system of equations and is heavier than the other mask nodes.
Under the hood

Builds the matting Laplacian from local RGB covariance windows (radius window_radius, regulariser epsilon) and solves (L + lambda D) alpha = lambda b, where D marks the trimap's known pixels and b their known alpha. The CPU path uses SciPy sparse solvers with a conjugate-gradient fallback. The GPU path builds a CUDA sparse matrix and runs a Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate gradient in PyTorch; if it fails (for example, out of memory) it warns and falls back to the CPU path. Each batch item is solved separately. A guide of batch 1 is broadcast. Source: core/mask_alpha_matte.py, trimap validation in core/mask_trimap.py.

docs.text:

  • Edge-Aware Mask Refiner for a lighter edge fix
  • Mask Preview for viewing the matte as a cutout
  • Mask Cleanup for cleaning the rough mask before building the trimap

docs.text: Alpha Matte example workflow. Copy workflows/sample_portrait.jpg and workflows/sample_binary_mask.png into ComfyUI/input/. It builds a trimap from the subject mask, shrinks the photo to 25% to keep matting fast, and solves the unknown band. With compute_device = auto a CPU image stays on the CPU; pick cuda on an NVIDIA GPU for roughly 5x speed. It uses only core ComfyUI nodes and this pack.

docs.title: Apply ColorLab Preset
docs.text:
Takes the settings from a ColorLab or Lightroom Preset node and applies the same look to another picture. One strength slider makes the look lighter or stronger, like the Amount slider on a Lightroom preset.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Color: Apply ColorLab Preset Good for Giving a batch of photos the look you built on one, toning a look down or up, applying a Lightroom preset at partial strength, grading only inside a mask

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
You grade one hero shot in ColorLab until it looks right. ColorLab's params_json output holds those settings as a preset. Connect it to this node and every image you feed in gets the same grade, without copying sliders by hand.

The strength slider scales the amounts of the preset, the way Lightroom's preset Amount does. Exposure, contrast, HSL, grading saturation and so on all shrink or grow together. Things that describe which colour or what shape stay the same: the grading hues (a teal shadow stays teal at any strength) and the shape settings of the vignette and grain. Point curves move toward a straight line as strength goes down.

It also accepts params_json from Lightroom Preset, so you can load a preset once and reuse it at different strengths.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → ColorLab. Grade the picture.
  2. Add Color: Apply ColorLab Preset. Connect ColorLab's params_json output to its params_json input.
  3. Connect the image (or batch) you want to grade to image, and image output → Preview Image.
  4. Start at strength 1.0, then try 0.5 to 0.8 for a softer version.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image The picture or batch to grade. params_json The preset, as ColorLab settings. Connection only: from ColorLab, Lightroom Preset, or a text node holding a saved preset. Invalid JSON stops the run with an error; unknown setting names are ignored with a warning. strength 1.0 0 to 2. Scales every amount in the preset. 0 returns the original image unchanged; above 1 pushes the look further. 0.5 to 0.8 for a subtle look, 1.2 to 1.5 to exaggerate a weak preset. mask (optional) none Applies the preset only where the mask is white, with soft edges where it is grey. It must be the same size as the image. Build it with Luminosity Masking or a subject mask.

What strength does not scale:

  • Grading hues (grade_*_hue): the tint colour stays the same, only its strength changes.
  • Vignette midpoint, feather and roundness, and grain size and roughness: the shape stays, the amount scales.
  • On/off and text settings: gray_enable, exposure_mode, tone_engine. A black-and-white preset fades in instead: below strength 1 the black-and-white result is blended over the colour one, so 0.5 keeps about half the colour (like Lightroom's preset Amount).

Outputs

Output What it is image The image with the preset applied. params_json The preset at the chosen strength. Save it, or connect it to ColorLab to fine-tune it with sliders.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• For a series (a wedding, a product shoot), grade the most typical frame, then batch the rest through this node. Check the darkest and brightest frames before you trust the look on all of them.
  • A preset made on a bright photo can look heavy on a dark one. Lower strength instead of rebuilding the grade.
  • Connect params_json to a ColorLab's params_json input when one frame needs a small fix: ColorLab adds its sliders on top of the preset.
  • Feed only the original image here, not one that ColorLab has already graded, or the look is applied twice.
  • Already have the look as a .cube file instead of ColorLab settings? Use LUT Import, which also has a strength slider and a mask input.
Under the hood

The preset is read with the same rules as ColorLab's params_json input, starting from neutral. Every number is multiplied by strength, except grading hues and the vignette and grain shape settings. Point curves are blended toward the identity line: each point [x, y] becomes [x, x + (y - x) · strength]. The scaled settings then run through the full ColorLab pipeline (core/color_lab.py, scale_params_json and apply_colorlab_pipeline). With strength 0 the input image is returned as is. With a mask, the result is original + (graded - original) · mask; the mask must be shaped (B, H, W) with the image's height and width, otherwise the node raises an error. The params_json output only lists values that differ from neutral.

docs.title: Auto Align
docs.text:
Finds the same points in two photos, works out how one must move, rotate or tilt to match the other, and warps it into place. No manual markers needed.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → geometry → Geometry: Auto Align Good for Lining up exposure brackets, before/after retouch pairs, and shots that must match a reference before a colour match or layer blend

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: Use it whenever two images show the same scene but are not pixel-aligned, for example handheld shots or a crop and an original. Align first, then compare or blend: Color Matcher and Layer Add work much better when both images show the same content in the same place.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect the picture to move to image and the target frame to reference.
  2. Keep method = sift and model = homography.
  3. Look at aligned in Preview Image, and check that inliers is comfortably above min_inliers.
  4. Use valid_mask to ignore the empty borders.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Setting Default What it does Tip image — The image to warp. reference — The target frame. The output has this size. One image, or the same batch size as image. method sift sift: classic keypoints, no download. loftr: learned matcher for hard pairs. LoFTR downloads about 45 MB on first use. model homography homography handles perspective change. affine allows rotate, scale, shear and shift only. affine is steadier for flat scenes or few matches. max_side 1024 (256 to 2048) Longest side used for matching. The final warp uses full resolution. Lower is faster. ransac_threshold 3.0 (0.5 to 20) How many pixels (at matching size) a match may be off and still count. Raise for slightly blurry pairs, lower for a tight fit. min_inliers 12 (4 to 500) Fewer agreeing matches than this triggers the fallback. Output Type Meaning aligned IMAGE image warped to the reference size. valid_mask MASK 1 where the warp has real pixels, 0 where the frame is empty. matrix_json STRING The 3×3 transform (one per image in a batch) in full-resolution pixels. inliers INT Number of agreeing matches for the first image in the batch.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• sift or loftr: start with sift. Try loftr when SIFT finds few matches (big lighting change, soft focus, repeated textures).
  • valid_mask: after a rotation or shift the edges of aligned are black. Use the mask to crop, feather, or restrict where a colour match reads its statistics.
  • If the node cannot find enough agreeing matches it does not stop. It logs a warning, resizes the image to the reference size and returns an all-white valid_mask. Always check inliers.
  • Moving subjects (people, leaves) are ignored as long as the background has enough texture.
  • For batches, inliers only reports the first image; check the others in matrix_json (a pure scale matrix means that image used the fallback).
Under the hood

Both images become grayscale copies shrunk to max_side. SIFT extracts keypoints and keeps mutual nearest-neighbour matches; LoFTR runs a neural network. RANSAC fits the chosen model on random subsets and keeps the fit most matches agree with, then the inliers are refitted by least squares and the matrix is scaled back to full resolution. The warp is bilinear (Kornia warp_perspective). valid_mask is the same warp applied to an all-ones image. Source: core/auto_align.py and nodes/auto_align_node.py.

docs.title: Auto Blemish
docs.text:
Detects the faces in a portrait and heals pimples, spots and small marks on the skin. The skin texture continues through each healed spot, so it does not look smoothed.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → face → Face: Auto Blemish Good for A first pass of spot healing on portraits, group photos, batches of headshots, body skin with your own mask Speed About 5 s on a CPU for an 8 MP portrait, under 1.1 GB VRAM

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
This is the automatic version of the Spot Healing Brush. It does the dull part of portrait retouching: finding every small mark. You then check the result and fix what remains by hand.

Warning

It also removes natural moles unless you protect them. Draw a mask over any beauty mark, freckle pattern or tattoo you want to keep and connect it to protect_mask.

Each face is processed in its own crop, with its own spot size, so group photos work. Eyes, brows and the mouth are never touched. For skin without a face in the frame (back, hands, arms), give the node a mask of the skin area instead.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Face: Auto Blemish → Preview Image.
  2. Keep the defaults. Raise sensitivity if faint marks are left. Lower it if freckles start to disappear.
  3. Connect spot_mask to Mask Preview to see exactly what was healed.
  4. Check face_count. If it is 0 on a portrait, the face was not found; use mask instead.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image The portrait to retouch. sensitivity 0.5 0 to 1. Higher catches fainter marks. Very high also removes freckles. 0.3 to 0.6 for most portraits. spot_scale 1.0 0.25 to 4. The largest mark to remove, relative to the automatic size (5 % of each face width). Raise it for bigger pimples. Lower it to keep small features. mask (optional) Skin area to clean instead of the detected faces. Spot size then follows the mask width. For body, back and hands. protect_mask (optional) Areas that are never touched. A beauty mark you keep, tattoos.

Outputs

Output What it is image The retouched image. spot_mask The pixels that were healed. Check it with Mask Preview. face_count How many faces were found. 0 when a mask is given.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Always look at spot_mask once. It shows whether the node caught real blemishes or something you want to keep.
  • Natural moles and strong freckles are at risk at high sensitivity. Protect them with protect_mask.
  • Follow with Skin Smoother or Frequency Separation for tone evening. Auto Blemish only removes marks.
  • A mark that survived is often bigger than the automatic limit. Raise spot_scale, or heal it with Heal / Content-Aware Fill.
  • Large images work well: each face is cropped, so cost depends on the faces, not the whole frame.
Under the hood
  1. Region. Face Detect Lite (YuNet) finds the faces. The weights are downloaded once by Kornia. Each face box, grown by 25 %, is processed as its own crop. Only skin-coloured pixels are kept (a soft YCrCb test that covers light to dark skin), minus discs around the eyes, brows and mouth placed from the five landmarks. A user mask replaces the face search.
  2. Detection. The spot detector of Dust & Spot Removal runs on a signal made of luma darkening plus redness, because pimples are redder more than they are darker. The largest spot follows the face size (about 5 % of the face width).
  3. Healing. The texture fill of Dust & Spot copies the best nearby skin patch, matched on the ring and brightness-corrected, so pores continue.

Source: core/blemish.py, wrapper nodes/blemish_node.py.

  • Dust & Spot Removal: the spot engine used here, for sensor dust
  • Face Detect Lite: the face detector used here
  • Skin Smoother: even out skin tone after cleaning
  • Mask Preview: see what was healed

docs.title: Auto Tone
docs.text:
Measures the photo and applies a first-pass correction: exposure, whites, blacks, highlights, shadows and white balance. It also gives you the settings it used, so you can keep editing them in ColorLab.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Auto: Tone & White Balance Good for A fast starting point for a batch, fixing dark or colour-cast photos, a quick automatic black and white Speed About 1.5 s per 4K image, VRAM about 1 GB

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Use it like the Auto button in Lightroom: you get a sensible base, then adjust by hand. The result is not final. The params_json output holds every setting that was applied, as ColorLab keys, so you can see exactly what changed and refine it.

It is careful on purpose:

  • A dark photo is brightened, but a bright high-key photo or a white background stays bright.
  • White balance looks only at pixels that are close to grey. Skin, foliage and sunsets never pull it. A photo with no grey in it is left alone.

Note

The constants are hand-tuned on test photos. They are not fitted to Adobe's Auto, and the node does not claim to match Lightroom.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Auto: Tone & White Balance → Preview Image.
  2. Keep the defaults. Lower strength (try 0.6) if the correction feels too strong.
  3. To fine-tune, connect params_json to the params_json input of ColorLab. Its sliders add on top of the automatic settings.
  4. To reuse the same settings on other photos, connect params_json to Apply ColorLab Preset.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image The photo or batch to correct. Each image of a batch is measured and corrected on its own. strength 1.0 0 to 1. How much of the automatic correction to apply. 0 returns the original. 0.5 to 0.8 for a lighter touch. exposure (optional) on Fixes overall brightness. Turn off if the brightness is already right. tone (optional) on Sets Whites, Blacks, Highlights and Shadows. white_balance (optional) on Removes colour casts using near-grey areas. Turn off for scenes lit by deliberately coloured light. black_and_white (optional) off Converts to black and white with an automatic grey mix. Brighter colour bands become brighter grey, which keeps colour contrast as tonal contrast. max_wb_shift (optional) 50 0 to 100. The largest Temp/Tint change white balance may make. Lower it for sunsets, candlelight and other intended warm or cool light.

Outputs

Output What it is image The corrected image, same size as the input. params_json The ColorLab settings that were applied, including tone_engine = local and exposure_mode = linear. Only the first image of a batch.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Run Auto Upright first, then this node, so the measurement sees the final framing.
  • Auto Tone suits a batch of similar photos as a starting grade. For a consistent look, grade one frame, then reuse its settings with Apply ColorLab Preset.
  • A strong warm or cool cast that is part of the mood (golden hour, tungsten) is best protected by a low max_wb_shift or by turning white_balance off.
  • A scene with no neutral objects gets little or no white balance change. This is intended; set Temp and Tint by hand in ColorLab.
  • If shadows still look heavy afterwards, add Shadows/Highlights Pro or CLAHE Local Contrast.
Under the hood

Everything is measured on a copy whose long edge is at most 512 px, so the result does not depend on image size. Source: core/auto_tone.py, wrapper nodes/auto_tone_node.py.

Exposure: from the log-average brightness, steering toward a 12 % key, a little below mid-grey, so moody and low-key photos keep their mood. Dark photos are brightened by up to +1 EV, limited so the brightest 0.5 % does not clip by more than half a stop. Bright photos are darkened only when really overexposed (up to -1 EV). When 40 % or more of the frame is near-white (product on white, high-key studio), only the rest of the photo (the subject) is judged, and it is darkened only if the subject itself is too bright; an all-white frame is left alone. Tiny corrections are skipped.

White balance: the mean colour of near-grey pixels in linear light, found over several rounds with a widening tolerance. The correction is scaled by the share of near-grey pixels, damped, and limited by max_wb_shift.

Tone: Whites and Blacks move the brightest and darkest 0.5 % of pixels toward fixed targets. Highlights and Shadows follow how much of the picture is near clipping.

Black and white: each colour band is made brighter or darker in grey than the image average.

The settings are applied by the ColorLab pipeline with strength scaling them, the same as in Apply ColorLab Preset. ComfyUI hands the image over on the CPU.

docs.text: Auto Tone example workflow: a dark café photo goes through Auto Tone, then params_json drives a ColorLab with Vibrance +15 and is shown in a text preview. It uses only core ComfyUI nodes and this pack. Copy workflows/sample_cafe.jpg into ComfyUI/input/ (Pexels License).

docs.title: Auto Upright
docs.text:
Straightens a photo the way Lightroom's Upright does: it finds the lines in the picture, then levels the horizon or makes the building verticals parallel. If it is not sure, it leaves the photo alone.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → geometry → Auto: Upright Good for Tilted horizons, buildings shot looking up, interiors, architecture and real-estate photos Speed About 0.1 to 0.3 s per image, VRAM under 0.3 GB

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Tilt the camera up at a building and the vertical lines lean toward each other. Hold the camera slightly rolled and the horizon is crooked. This node measures both from the straight lines in the photo and corrects them with no sliders to guess.

It only acts when the evidence is clear. Portraits, trees, clouds or noisy scenes have no reliable lines, so the image comes back unchanged and confidence is 0. A wrong guess would be worse than no correction.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Auto: Upright → Preview Image.
  2. Keep mode on auto. Set crop to valid for a clean final image.
  3. If a tall building looks too rigid, lower strength to about 0.7.
  4. Watch the confidence output (connect it to a text preview). 0 means nothing was changed.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image The photo or batch to straighten. mode auto auto = parallel verticals if buildings are found, otherwise a level horizon. level = rotate only. vertical = parallel verticals. full = verticals plus the main horizontal lines. level for landscapes and seascapes. full for a facade seen straight on. strength 1.0 0 to 1. The fraction of the correction to apply. About 0.7 keeps a natural bit of perspective in tall buildings. crop none none keeps everything, with black corners where the picture was turned. valid zooms in until no empty corners remain. valid for final output. max_angle (optional) 25 0 to 45 degrees. Larger corrections stop at this angle. Steep look-up shots are corrected part of the way instead of being stretched too far.

Outputs

Output What it is image The straightened image, same size as the input. confidence 0 to 1, the lowest value of a batch. 0 means the image was left unchanged. matrix Text (JSON) list of the 3x3 pixel transforms that were applied, one per image.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Run Auto Upright before Auto Tone and other colour work, so you measure the final framing.
  • With crop set to none, the corners go black. Use valid, or crop yourself, before you send the picture on.
  • Strong wide-angle distortion bends lines too. If lines curve near the edges, fix that first with Lens Distortion.
  • Use level when the scene has only a horizon and no buildings. It will not invent a perspective change.
  • A confidence of 0 usually means the photo has too few long straight lines, or its verticals lean more than 15 degrees, which are not treated as walls. Straighten it by hand or try level.
Under the hood

Straight line segments are found with OpenCV's line segment detector on a copy whose long edge is at most 1024 px. Source: core/upright.py, wrapper nodes/upright_node.py.

level: the tilt is the length-weighted median of the near-horizontal and near-vertical lines, and the photo is rotated about its centre.

vertical / full: vanishing points are found by RANSAC, then refined. The camera is virtually rotated (H = K·R·K⁻¹) so the vertical vanishing point goes to infinity and the verticals become parallel. full also does this for the main horizontal point. Focal length comes from the two points when they are orthogonal, otherwise a default of about a 36 mm lens.

Safety gate: level needs at least 3 lines, enough total length and 60 % of that length in agreement. A vanishing point needs at least 5 lines and agreeing lines totalling half the long edge. Lines leaning more than 15 degrees are not treated as walls. Otherwise the image is returned unchanged with confidence 0.

The warp runs with Kornia on the image's device. crop valid zooms to the largest rectangle of the original shape that holds only image pixels.

docs.text:

  • Lens Distortion: remove barrel or pincushion bending before straightening
  • Auto Align: align a series of photos to each other

docs.title: CLAHE Local Contrast
docs.text:
Opens up dark areas and adds definition to flat ones by adjusting contrast tile by tile, on lightness only, so hue and colour do not shift.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Color: CLAHE Local Contrast Good for Lifting murky shadows, rescuing hazy or flat shots, adding crunch to product and texture detail

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
CLAHE (Contrast Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalisation) looks at small tiles of the picture and spreads out the brightness values inside each one, with a limit so noise is not blown up. The result feels like strong local contrast: dark corners gain detail and flat surfaces gain depth.

Here it runs only on the lightness channel of the CIE LAB colour space, so colours are not touched. Running it on RGB channels, as many tools do, shifts colours and tints skin.

Compared with the basic_clarity slider in ColorLab: clarity is a gentle, radius-based punch for edges. CLAHE redistributes brightness inside each tile, so it can lift deep shadows and flatten large soft gradients that clarity leaves alone. Use clarity for gentle punch, CLAHE when a region is too flat, too dark or too hazy.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → CLAHE Local Contrast → Preview Image.
  2. Leave clip_limit at 2.0 and grid_size at 8.
  3. Lower strength to about 0.5 for portraits, then compare with the original.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image required The picture to enhance. clip_limit 2.0 (0.1 to 40) How strongly each tile may be stretched. Higher means more contrast and more noise. 1.5 to 3 for most work; above about 6 grain jumps out. grid_size 8 (2 to 32) Number of tiles across and down. Fewer tiles give a broad, natural lift; more tiles give a crunchy, detailed look. 4 to 6 natural, 12 to 24 gritty. strength 1.0 (0 to 1) Blend between the original (0) and the CLAHE result (1). 0.3 to 0.6 for portraits. mask (optional) none Limits where the effect applies. A single mask is used for the whole batch. Keep faces or skies out of the effect.

Output: image, the enhanced picture.

On small images the grid is reduced automatically so that every tile is at least 80 px wide. Images smaller than 80 px come back unchanged.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Start gentle. clip_limit 2 at strength 0.5 is often better than 4 at full strength.
  • For portraits, mask out the face and apply it to clothing, hair or background only; skin rarely likes this much local contrast.
  • If shadows turn grainy, lower clip_limit first, then strength.
  • Combine with Smart Sharpen afterwards for crisp edges, and apply Tone Curve last for the final contrast shape.
  • Flat colour areas stay flat, so solid backgrounds do not get tinted.
Under the hood

The image is converted to CIE LAB (Kornia). Only L* (divided by 100) goes through kornia.enhance.equalize_clahe on a grid_size × grid_size tile grid; the original a* and b* are kept, the result is converted back to RGB and clamped to 0..1. The final image is lerp(original, enhanced, strength × mask). Kornia works with 256-bin histograms, so L* is quantised to 256 levels. Its clip threshold biases very small tiles (a flat image can drift brighter), which is why tiles are kept at 80 px or more. strength = 0 returns the original.

docs.text:

  • Smart Sharpen: edge sharpening after the contrast lift
  • Tone Curve: shape global contrast
  • Luminosity Masking: restrict the effect to shadows or highlights

docs.title: ColorLab
docs.text:
A full Camera Raw style finishing stage in a single node: white balance, exposure and tone, per-colour HSL, three-way colour grading with colour wheels and a black-and-white mixer. Every control starts at neutral, and the settings can be passed on as a preset.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Color: ColorLab (ACR) Good for A quick global grade, teal-and-orange looks, split toning, black-and-white conversion, one-node finishing after retouching, grading once and reusing the look on other photos Speed With tone_engine set to local, a 4K image takes about 0.2 s on the GPU with a peak of about 1.56 GB.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
If you know Lightroom or Camera Raw, you already know this node. Instead of chaining many small nodes, you get the same panels in the same order, applied as one pipeline: White balance → Basic → HSL → Color Grading → B&W (Gray Mix). It is a good final step after the heavy retouching is done, or a stand-in for a Camera Raw pass on a generated image.

It is an approximation written for this pack, not Adobe's code, so numbers will not match Camera Raw one-to-one. Judge by eye. With every slider at 0 and B&W off, the image passes through untouched.

The node has 59 controls plus an optional params_json input. Their names tell you the panel: basic_*, wb_*, hsl_*, grade_*, gray_*.

docs.title: The tabbed panel
docs.text:
To keep the node short, the controls are grouped in tabs: Basic, HSL, Grading, B&W and Options.

  • Basic holds the Light and Presence sliders, plus Temp and Tint under White balance.
  • HSL shows a row of 8 colour dots. Click a dot to pick a colour; its Hue, Saturation and Luminance sliders appear below.
  • Grading shows three Lightroom-style wheels for Shadows, Midtones and Highlights. Drag inside a wheel: the angle sets the hue, the distance from the centre sets the saturation. Click the centre for no tint. Below the wheels you get Hue, Saturation, Luminance and Balance sliders for the selected region.
  • B&W holds Convert to B&W and the per-colour gray mix sliders.
  • Options holds exposure_mode and tone_engine.
  • A small blue dot marks every tab (and every HSL colour or grading wheel) that has edits.
  • Reset sets the open tab back to neutral. On HSL and Grading it only resets the colour or region you are looking at.

Workflows saved before the tabs existed open on the first tab that has edits. The tabs only change the display: the values saved in your workflow and sent in API prompts are exactly the same as before. If you use ComfyUI's Vue nodes mode, the node shows the plain list of sliders instead.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → ColorLab → Preview Image.
  2. On the Basic tab, nudge Exposure and Contrast, then Highlights and Shadows. Fix a colour cast with Temp and Tint.
  3. For colour, move on to HSL or Grading. Change one tab at a time and compare against the original.
  4. For black and white, open B&W, turn on Convert to B&W and shape the tones with the colour sliders.
  5. Want highlights and shadows that behave more like Lightroom? On Options, set tone_engine to local.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: All sliders default to 0, except where noted. "±100" means the slider runs from -100 to 100.

docs.title: Basic
docs.text:
Global tone and presence (the Basic tab).

Setting Range What it does basic_exposure -5 to 5 (stops) Overall brightness. Each +1 doubles the light. basic_contrast ±100 Spreads tones away from mid-grey. With the local engine it is an S-curve that keeps pure black and pure white in place. basic_highlights ±100 Brightens or recovers the bright half of the picture. basic_shadows ±100 Opens up or deepens the dark half. basic_whites ±100 Moves the very brightest tones. basic_blacks ±100 Moves the very darkest tones. basic_texture ±100 Fine-detail punch (small radius). basic_clarity ±100 Mid-tone local contrast (larger radius), strongest in the mid-tones. basic_dehaze ±100 Cuts haze; negative adds a soft haze. basic_vibrance ±100 Boosts weak colours more than strong ones and protects skin tones. basic_saturation ±100 Scales all colours equally.

docs.title: White balance
docs.text:
Shown as Temp and Tint on the Basic tab. Both are optional and relative: they shift the colour of the picture you already have, they are not Kelvin values.

Setting Range What it does wb_temperature ±100 Warmer (+) or cooler (-). wb_tint ±100 Magenta (+) or green (-).

Brightness is kept while the colour shifts, so a white balance change does not make the picture lighter or darker.

docs.title: HSL
docs.text:
Eight colour bands: red, orange, yellow, green, aqua, blue, purple, magenta. Each has three sliders named hsl_<colour>_hue, hsl_<colour>_sat and hsl_<colour>_lum, all ±100 (24 in total, e.g. hsl_orange_sat). On the HSL tab, pick the colour with its dot.

Slider What it does hsl_<colour>_hue Rotates that colour toward its neighbours (up to about 30 degrees at the extremes). hsl_<colour>_sat Makes that colour stronger or weaker. hsl_<colour>_lum Makes that colour lighter or darker.

Bands overlap softly, so neighbouring colours move a little with the one you edit. This is the panel for teal-and-orange, greener foliage or calmer skin reds.

docs.title: Color Grading
docs.text:
Three tonal ranges: shadow, mid, highlight. Each has four sliders, named grade_<range>_hue, grade_<range>_sat, grade_<range>_lum and grade_<range>_bal (12 in total, e.g. grade_shadow_hue). On the Grading tab, the wheels set hue and sat for you.

Slider Range What it does grade_<range>_hue 0 to 360 The tint colour, as a position on the colour wheel. grade_<range>_sat 0 to 100 How strong the tint is. The tint only appears when this is above 0. grade_<range>_lum ±100 Lightens or darkens that tonal range. grade_<range>_bal ±100 Treats pixels as brighter (positive) or darker (negative) when deciding which range they belong to. Positive shrinks the shadow range and widens the highlight range.

Set hue first, then raise sat slowly. A touch of blue in the shadows and warm yellow in the highlights is the classic split-tone.

docs.title: Gray Mix (B&W)
docs.text:
Black-and-white conversion with per-colour control (the B&W tab).

Setting Default Range What it does gray_enable off on / off Converts the image to grey (Convert to B&W). Nothing in this panel applies while it is off. gray_red, gray_orange, gray_yellow, gray_green, gray_aqua, gray_blue, gray_purple 0 -200 to 300 How light each colour appears in the grey result. Positive lightens that colour, negative darkens it.

There is no gray_magenta slider: magenta follows its neighbours unless a preset sets it (see below).

docs.title: Options
docs.text: Setting Default What it does exposure_mode (optional) display display multiplies the picture values by 2^EV (the classic ColorLab behaviour). linear converts to linear light first, multiplies, then converts back, like a camera or Lightroom. tone_engine (optional) legacy legacy keeps the behaviour of earlier versions. local makes Highlights and Shadows edge-aware (they follow the shapes in the picture instead of shifting whole tonal bands), uses an edge-aware Clarity, a dark-channel Dehaze and a Contrast S-curve that keeps black and white. It runs on the GPU when one is available.

docs.title: The params_json input
docs.text:
params_json (optional, connection only) takes ColorLab settings as text, for example from Color: Lightroom Preset (XMP) or from another ColorLab's params_json output.

  • Numbers are added to the sliders. The preset sets the starting point and the sliders on this node fine-tune it: a preset with Exposure 0.5 plus a slider at 0.2 gives 0.7.
  • On/off switches and text settings (gray_enable, exposure_mode, tone_engine) replace the node's value.
  • Unknown names are ignored with a warning in the console. Text that is not a valid JSON object stops the run with an error.

docs.title: Settings that only come from params_json
docs.text:
These settings have no slider. They arrive through params_json, usually from a Lightroom preset or from a preset saved from ColorLab.

Setting Values What it does tone_curve list of [x, y] points, 0 to 255 Point curve on all channels, like Lightroom's Point Curve. tone_curve_red, tone_curve_green, tone_curve_blue list of [x, y] points, 0 to 255 Point curve on one channel. Curves need at least two points with different x. calib_red_hue, calib_red_sat, calib_green_hue, calib_green_sat, calib_blue_hue, calib_blue_sat, calib_shadow_tint ±100 Calibration panel: shifts the hue and saturation of the red, green and blue primaries, and the green/magenta tint of the deep shadows. vignette_amount, vignette_midpoint, vignette_feather, vignette_roundness amount ±100 (negative darkens the corners) Post-crop vignette. Midpoint, feather and roundness default to 50, 50 and 0. grain_amount, grain_size, grain_frequency amount 0 to 100 Film grain on brightness. Size and roughness default to 25 and 50. The grain pattern is the same on every run. gray_magenta -200 to 300 Magenta slider of the B&W mix. When it is not set, magenta follows its neighbours.

Outputs

Output What it is image The adjusted picture. params_json This node's settings as a preset: only the values that differ from neutral, including anything that came in through params_json. Connect it to another ColorLab's params_json or to Apply ColorLab Preset.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• For natural exposure moves, set exposure_mode to linear. Real light adds up in linear space, so +1 stop behaves like opening the camera aperture one stop: mid-grey 0.5 goes to about 0.69, highlights roll off gradually and colours keep their balance. display multiplies the stored values instead, so the same +1 sends mid-grey to 1.0 and clips bright areas quickly. Old workflows stay on display.
  • Recovering a bright sky or opening a backlit face? Try tone_engine = local. The legacy engine lifts or pulls whole tonal bands, which can flatten the picture; the local engine works around edges, so detail and local contrast survive.
  • Work top to bottom: white balance and tone in Basic first, colour in HSL or Grading afterwards, so the colour edits sit on a stable base.
  • Use small steps. Many sliders act strongly near their ends; 10 to 30 is often plenty.
  • Skin mostly sits in the orange band. Move hsl_orange_* gently and shift blues and greens harder when you want a look without sickly skin.
  • For black and white, darken gray_blue to deepen skies, lighten gray_orange and gray_red to smooth skin.
  • Grade one hero shot, then send its params_json to Apply ColorLab Preset to give a whole batch the same look.
  • When you chain two ColorLab nodes, connect either the image or the params_json from the first one, not both. Feeding both applies the grade twice.
  • ColorLab affects the whole frame. To grade only part of it, blend the result back through a mask (see Luminosity Masking), or use the mask input of Apply ColorLab Preset.
  • Want only local contrast? CLAHE Local Contrast lifts flat or dark regions in a different way than basic_clarity.
Under the hood

The pipeline lives in core/color_lab.py and uses plain PyTorch plus Kornia. Input is clamped to 0..1. The order is: white balance → calibration → Basic → point curves → HSL → Color Grading → Gray Mix → vignette → grain.

  • White balance: in linear light, red is scaled by 1 + 0.3·temp, green by 1 - 0.22·tint, blue by 1 - 0.3·temp, then the result is rescaled to the original luminance (Rec. 709).
  • Calibration: a 3×3 linear-RGB matrix that rotates the hue and scales the chroma of each primary in OkLCh while keeping white fixed; Shadows Tint changes green in the deep shadows with luminance kept.
  • Basic, legacy engine: exposure multiplies by 2^exposure (display, on the sRGB values) or converts to linear RGB with Kornia, multiplies by 2^exposure, clamps and converts back (linear; mid-grey 0.5 at +1 EV becomes about 0.686); contrast pivots around 0.5; highlights, shadows, whites and blacks add smoothstep-weighted offsets driven by luma (Rec. 601 weights) and are range-protected so they do not clip; texture and clarity are unsharp-style boosts using a 5 px and a 9 px box blur with replicated borders (clarity is weighted toward the mid-tones); dehaze is a contrast and offset change; vibrance and saturation work in HSV, with vibrance down-weighted near the skin hue.
  • Basic, local engine: dehaze runs first, with a dark-channel prior (He et al. 2009) and an airlight estimated from a 512 px proxy; contrast is the S-curve x - a·sin(2πx)/2π (black and white fixed); highlights and shadows use a local Laplacian filter; clarity boosts a band of log luminance split off with a guided filter, weighted to the mid-tones. Whites, blacks, texture, vibrance and saturation are the same as in legacy. When the image is on the CPU and a CUDA GPU is available, the pipeline moves to the GPU and back; if the GPU runs out of memory it falls back to the CPU.
  • Point curves: monotone cubic (Fritsch-Carlson) curves, flat beyond the end points; the master curve first, then the per-channel curves.
  • HSL: each band is a Gaussian on the hue circle (sigma 20 degrees) around fixed anchors: red 0, orange 30, yellow 60, green 120, aqua 180, blue 240, purple 280, magenta 310.
  • Color Grading: each range uses a smooth luma mask (shifted by bal), a tint built from hue and sat, and lum as a lift.
  • Gray Mix: luma is modulated by the per-band weights; magenta only joins when gray_magenta is set.
  • Vignette and grain run last, in Lightroom's order. Grain uses a fixed seed.

The result is passed through nan_to_num and clamped to 0..1. If all settings are neutral and gray_enable is off, the input is returned as is. With the new inputs left at their defaults the output is the same as in earlier versions.

docs.title: Color Matcher Region
docs.text:
Matches colour between two chosen areas, for example the skin of a generated face to the skin of the original plate, or the sky of one shot to the sky of another.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Color Matcher Region (LAB) Good for Skin-to-skin matching, sky or background matching, matching a retouched area to a different photo

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: Color Matcher compares the whole of two same-size pictures. Often that is not what you want: a face swap has skin next to a blue wall, and the reference may be a different crop entirely. Color Matcher Region lets you draw a mask on each side. The colour "character" (average and spread) is measured only inside the reference mask, and used to recolour only the area inside the target mask. Because only statistics are compared, the two pictures do not need the same size or framing.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect your edit to image_target and the picture with the colours you want to image_reference.
  2. Make a mask over the area to fix (for example with Skin Tone Tri-Region) and connect it to target_mask.
  3. Make a mask over the matching area of the reference and connect it to reference_mask.
  4. Keep channels on ab, set strength around 0.8, and preview image_matched.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image_target required The picture to recolour. image_reference required The picture that provides the colours. Can be a different size. channels ab ab matches colour only and keeps the target's brightness. lab matches brightness as well. ab for skin and products. strength 1.0 (0 to 1) 0 leaves the image untouched, 1 applies the full match. 0.6 to 0.9 for natural results. target_mask (optional) whole image Area of the target that is measured and recoloured. Soft edges give soft transitions. Must match the target's size. Feather hard selections first. reference_mask (optional) whole image Area of the reference that is measured. Must match the reference's size. Pick a clean, evenly lit patch. method (optional) stats stats matches the average and spread of each channel (smooth, safe). histogram matches the whole distribution of each channel, so shadows, mid-tones and highlights each land where the reference has them. Try histogram when stats gets close but not quite there.

Output: image_matched, the recoloured image. Outside target_mask the picture is unchanged.

docs.title: Stats or histogram?
docs.text:
• stats (default) shifts and stretches each channel so its average and spread equal the reference's. It is gentle and predictable, and the right choice for most skin and white-balance fixes.
  • histogram reshapes each channel so its whole distribution (the histogram) follows the reference's. It fixes cases where two pictures share an average but feel different, for example a flat render against a contrasty photo. It is stronger, so lower strength and watch for exaggerated noise or banding in smooth areas.

Old workflows keep working: when method is absent, stats is used.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• For faces, use ab: lighting and skin texture stay intact, only the colour shifts.
  • Keep the reference patch free of shadows, glasses, lipstick or hair; one clean cheek is better than the whole face.
  • Soften hard masks before use. Mask Edge Smoother or Sub-Pixel Mask Refiner avoid a visible seam at the border.
  • To match the whole frame between same-size pictures, the simpler Color Matcher is enough.
Under the hood

Both images go to CIE LAB (Kornia). Mean and standard deviation of the selected channels are computed with mask weights inside each mask, then the target is shifted and scaled to the reference's statistics (Reinhard transfer). The result is converted back to RGB, blended by strength, and finally composited with lerp(target, matched, target_mask). Each mask must have the same height and width as its own image and contain at least one positive pixel; a single mask or reference is broadcast over a batch. Masks and images outside 0..1 are clamped with a logged warning.

With method = histogram, each selected channel of the target and of the reference is binned into a 4096-bin histogram (weighted by the mask when there is one). Every target pixel is mapped to its quantile in the target CDF, then to the value at the same quantile in the reference CDF (linear interpolation inside bins). The blend by strength and the output path are the same as stats. It runs on the GPU in a few milliseconds at 2K and stays well under 1 GB.
