docs.text: Color Matcher stats vs histogram example workflow matches a cool shot to a warm reference with both methods side by side (shown with Color Matcher; the Region node has the same method switch). It uses only core ComfyUI nodes and this pack. Copy workflows/sample_portrait.jpg into ComfyUI/input/.

docs.title: Color Matcher
docs.text:
Pulls the colours of a target image toward a reference image, the way you would match skin tones between two shots or pull an AI render back to the original plate.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Color Matcher (LAB) Good for Re-anchoring AI-generated skin to the source photo, matching a batch to one hero frame, harmonising inserts with a plate

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Two photos of the same subject rarely agree on colour: different white balance, different light, or an AI pass that drifted warm. Color Matcher measures the overall colour "character" of the reference (the average and the spread of each channel) and reshapes the target to match it. This is the classic Reinhard colour transfer, done in CIE LAB, a colour space built around how people see colour, with lightness (L) separated from the two colour axes (a and b).

By default only the colour axes are matched (ab). Brightness and contrast stay as they were, so lighting is not washed out. Switch to lab when you also want the reference's overall brightness.

Need to match only a part of the picture, or use images of different sizes? Use Color Matcher Region.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load the picture to fix with Load Image and connect it to image_target.
  2. Load the look you want with a second Load Image and connect it to image_reference. It must have the same width and height as the target.
  3. Leave channels on ab and set strength to about 0.7.
  4. Connect image_matched to Preview Image.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image_target required The picture that gets recoloured. image_reference required The picture whose colours you want. Same width and height as the target. A batch of 1 is reused for every target frame. channels ab ab matches colour only and keeps the target's brightness. lab matches brightness as well. Use ab for skin and product work. strength 1.0 (0 to 1) Blend between the original (0) and the full match (1). 0.6 to 0.8 looks most natural on skin. mask (optional) none A mask that decides which pixels are used to measure the colour statistics, on both images. See the note below. method (optional) stats stats matches the average and spread of each channel (smooth, safe). histogram matches the whole distribution of each channel, so shadows, mid-tones and highlights each land where the reference has them. Try histogram when stats gets close but not quite there.

Output: image_matched, the recoloured image.

The mask picks what is measured, not where the result lands

The mask is used to measure the colour statistics (for example, only the skin pixels of both pictures). The resulting colour change is still applied to the whole target frame. To limit where the change shows up, use Color Matcher Region or blend the result back with a mask in your own chain.

docs.title: Stats or histogram?
docs.text:
• stats (default) shifts and stretches each channel so its average and spread equal the reference's. It is gentle and predictable, and the right choice for most skin and white-balance fixes.
  • histogram reshapes each channel so its whole distribution (the histogram) follows the reference's. It fixes cases where two pictures share an average but feel different, for example a flat render against a contrasty photo. It is stronger, so lower strength and watch for exaggerated noise or banding in smooth areas.

Old workflows keep working: when method is absent, stats is used.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Keep channels on ab for portraits. lab also moves exposure and can flatten your lighting.
  • Use a mask over the skin on both pictures so a blue wall or green background does not skew the match.
  • Do not push strength to 1.0 when the two pictures are very different (warm indoor vs. cool daylight). Go in at 0.6 and judge by the skin.
  • Run it before the final grade, so Tone Curve or ColorLab work on a consistent base.
Under the hood

Both images are converted with Kornia rgb_to_lab. For the chosen channels, the target is shifted and scaled so its mean and standard deviation equal the reference's: (target − mean_t) × (std_ref / std_t) + mean_ref. With a mask, mean and standard deviation are mask-weighted. The result is converted back to RGB, cleaned of NaN and clamped to 0..1, then blended with the original by strength. strength = 0 returns the input unchanged. Reference and target must share height and width; a mask must match them too and contain at least one positive pixel. Inputs outside 0..1 are clamped with a logged warning.

With method = histogram, each selected channel of the target and of the reference is binned into a 4096-bin histogram (weighted by the mask when there is one). Every target pixel is mapped to its quantile in the target CDF, then to the value at the same quantile in the reference CDF (linear interpolation inside bins). The blend by strength and the output path are the same as stats. It runs on the GPU in a few milliseconds at 2K and stays well under 1 GB.

docs.title: Cull Score
docs.text:
Drop in a whole shoot. The node scores every frame, skips blurry, badly exposed and near-duplicate shots, and hands back the keepers, best first.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → qa → QA: Cull Score Good for Shortlisting a burst or a portrait session, removing blurry and blown-out frames, keeping one of several near-identical shots Speed Each photo is measured on a 1024 px copy, so the cost does not depend on the original size

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
After a shoot you often have dozens of near-identical frames. This node is a helper to shortlist them. It is not a judge of expression or composition, so look at the picks yourself before you deliver.

It checks four things: sharpness, exposure, closed eyes (when it finds faces) and duplicates. Sharpness is compared with the sharpest shot of the same scene, so a soft-looking portrait does not lose to a busy street photo that happens to be in the same batch.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load a batch of same-size photos (for example with Load Image Batch).
  2. Connect it to QA: Cull Score.
  3. Send selected to Preview Image or Save Image. Read report with a text display node if you want the numbers.
  4. Set top_k to the number of photos you want, or leave it at 0 to keep every photo that passes min_score.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip images A batch of photos, all the same size. top_k 0 0 to 1000. Keep at most this many photos. 0 keeps every photo that passes. Set it to 1 to get only the best frame. min_score 0.5 0 to 1. Drops photos scoring below this. Raise it for a stricter cull, lower it to keep more. check_eyes on Lowers the score of photos where a face has closed eyes. Needs MediaPipe, and is skipped if it is missing. Turn off for scenes without people.

Outputs

Output What it is selected The kept photos, best first. It is never empty: if nothing passes, the best photo is returned. report JSON with one entry per input photo: index, score, sharpness, exposure, eyes_closed, faces, duplicate_of, keep and energy. kept How many photos were kept (INT).

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• The score is 0.6 for sharpness and 0.4 for exposure, minus 0.4 if eyes are closed. Use report to see why a frame was dropped.
  • In report, duplicate_of shows which frame a near-identical shot was folded into. Only the best of each group is kept.
  • Photos in one batch must be the same size. Resize first if your shoot mixes sizes.
  • A blurred background with a sharp subject still counts as sharp. When faces are found, the face areas are measured instead.
  • Send selected on to the retouching chain, for example Auto Tone, so you only edit the keepers.
  • eyes_closed is null in the report when the eye check is off or MediaPipe is not available.
Under the hood

Every photo is measured on a 1024 px copy. Sharpness is Laplacian energy per tile of an 8 by 8 grid, taking the 90th percentile, so a sharp subject on a soft background still scores high. When faces are found (YuNet), the face boxes are measured instead. The value goes on a log scale and is compared with the sharpest shot of the same scene, found by a similar difference hash. A shot 10 times blurrier than that scores 0 for the relative part.

Exposure is penalised for clipped highlights, crushed shadows and an average far from mid-grey. Closed eyes use the eye aspect ratio (Soukupova and Cech, 2016) from MediaPipe landmarks, with 0.18 as the limit.

Duplicates are grouped with a 64-bit difference hash. Photos within 10 bits of each other form one group and only the best is kept. Source: core/cull.py, wrapper nodes/cull_node.py.

docs.title: Decontaminate Colors
docs.text:
Cleans the coloured fringe around a cut-out. When you place a subject on a new background, the edge pixels still carry the old background colour. This node replaces it with the subject's own colour.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → mask → Mask: Decontaminate Colors Good for Green-screen spill on hair, bright sky halos around a subject, any cut-out with a soft matte Speed About 0.9 GB VRAM at 4K.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A matte has soft edge pixels (mask values between 0 and 1). Each of those pixels is a mix of the subject and the old background. Once you put the subject on a new background, that mix shows as a green, blue or white fringe, most visible on hair.

This node estimates the subject's colour near each edge pixel and writes it back. You then composite with the decontaminated image and the same mask, for example with Mask Preview in cutout mode or the Layer nodes.

It cannot help a hard mask: if every mask value is exactly 0 or 1, nothing changes. Make a soft edge first with Alpha Matte, Sub-Pixel Mask Refiner or Edge-Aware Mask Refiner.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → a soft subject mask (Alpha Matte, or a refined mask).
  2. Connect the photo to image and the mask to mask of Mask: Decontaminate Colors.
  3. Start with radius 16 and strength 1.
  4. Composite the output image with the same mask over your new background and compare with the original.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip radius 16 1 to 256. How far, in pixels, the node looks for the subject's own colour. Raise it for wide, wispy edges such as hair. strength 1.0 0 to 1. 0 returns the image unchanged, 1 is the full correction. Lower it if the edge looks too clean next to the rest of the subject.

Output

Output What it is image The image with corrected edge colours. Pixels where the mask is exactly 0 or 1 are unchanged.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Always use the output image with the same mask. The mask still decides how much of the subject shows.
  • A wide, soft mask gives the node more to work with. Refine the edge first, then decontaminate.
  • Raise radius for long hair. Keep it low for crisp product edges.
  • Check the result on the final background, not on the original one: the fringe only shows there.
Under the hood

Edge pixels follow I = alpha × F + (1 − alpha) × B. The node estimates the subject colour from solid subject pixels (alpha at least 0.95) and the background colour from pixels with alpha at most 0.05 nearby, by normalised convolution. Where alpha is large it solves the equation for F, which keeps fine hair detail. Where alpha is small, that solve is unstable, so it uses the nearby subject colour instead. In between, the two blend. If no solid pixels are in reach, wider blurs fill in. The blurs run on a reduced copy and are scaled back up, so memory grows with the number of pixels only. Source: core/decontaminate.py.

docs.title: Defringe
docs.text:
Removes the purple or green outlines that appear along branches, backlit edges and chrome, and the red and cyan outlines toward the corners. Only the fringe pixels change. The rest of the picture stays as it was.

Note

The purple fringe in this example image was simulated on a sample photo, so you can see the effect clearly. Real fringes look similar but vary by lens.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Color: Defringe Good for Backlit branches and leaves against the sky, bright windows, chrome and metal highlights, wide-open lens shots Speed 4K stays under 1 GB VRAM

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Lenses focus colours slightly differently. That leaves two kinds of fringe:

  • Purple (or green) fringe. A coloured halo along strong light-dark edges. Common with wide-open lenses and backlight.
  • Lateral chromatic aberration. Red and blue are magnified slightly differently from green, so edges get red and cyan outlines that grow toward the corners.

Both are fixed here in one step. Lateral CA is lined up first, then the leftover coloured pixels along edges are pulled back to the colour next to them.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Color: Defringe → Preview Image.
  2. Keep the defaults: purple 1, green 0, lateral_ca on.
  3. Zoom in 100 % on a high-contrast edge and compare with the original.
  4. If green fringes remain on metal or glass, raise green to 0.5.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image Photo with coloured edges. purple 1.0 0 to 1. How strongly purple and magenta fringes next to strong edges are removed. Lower it if a real purple object loses colour at its edge. green 0.0 0 to 1. How strongly green fringes are removed. Off by default. Leaves seen against a bright sky can turn grey, so raise it only when green fringes are the problem. lateral_ca on Lines up the red and blue planes with green. The shift is measured automatically on a 1024 px copy and only applied when it clearly lines the edges up. Turn off if the lens was already corrected. radius (optional) 0 0 to 32 px. Fringe width. 0 means automatic: 0.15 % of the long edge. Raise it for wide fringes on very large files.

Output

Output What it is image The photo with fringes removed. Same size as the input.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Defringe before you sharpen, so Smart Sharpen does not strengthen the fringes.
  • If your raw converter already applied lens correction, turn lateral_ca off and keep only the fringe removal.
  • Branches against the sky usually need only purple. Add green for a purple-and-green pair, and look at the leaves before and after.
  • Leave radius on 0 first. Change it only if you can still see a fringe after the automatic pass.
  • Geometric lens distortion is a different problem. Use Lens Distortion for that.
Under the hood
  1. Lateral CA. The red and blue planes are scaled about the image centre by the factor that best lines their edges up with green. The factor is found by correlating high-pass planes on a 1024 px copy, searched over about plus or minus 0.4 %. It is applied at full size only when the edge correlation improves clearly.
  2. Fringe removal. A fringe pixel has a purple (270 to 335 degrees) or green (75 to 165 degrees) hue, is clearly coloured, and lies within radius of a strong luminance edge. Its Lab a* and b* move toward the colour of the nearby non-fringe pixels. Lightness is kept, so the edge stays sharp. Only fringe pixels change.

The image is processed in strips, which keeps 4K under 1 GB of VRAM. Source: core/defringe.py, wrapper nodes/defringe_node.py.

docs.title: Depth Anything V2
docs.text:
Turns a flat photo into a depth map: white is near the camera, black is far away. Use it to drive lens blur, fog, relighting or depth-based masks.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → depth → Depth: Depth Anything V2 Good for Fake depth of field, separating foreground from background, depth masks for colour grading

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A depth map is a greyscale picture where brightness means distance. Depth Anything V2 guesses it from one photo, with no stereo pair or sensor. The result is relative: it tells you what is nearer than what, not how many metres away it is. Values are normalised for each image, so 1 is the nearest thing in the frame and 0 the farthest.

Connect the depth output to Depth Lens Blur or to any node that takes a mask. depth_preview is the same map as a greyscale image for Preview Image.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Depth: Depth Anything V2 → Preview Image (use depth_preview).
  2. Keep model on small and resolution on 518.
  3. Wire depth into Depth Lens Blur.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
• Install onnxruntime once: pip install onnxruntime-gpu (or pip install onnxruntime for CPU only). Without it the node raises a clear error.
  • The model file is downloaded on first use into ComfyUI/models/depth_anything/ (or the depth_anything folder from extra_model_paths.yaml if you set one) as depth-anything-v2-<size>.onnx (small is about 99 MB). The folder is only created when a download starts. Downloads come from a fixed Hugging Face revision (not main) with a 60 s network timeout; the small model is also checked against its SHA256, while base and large are pinned by revision only. If the download is blocked, save the file there by hand from https://huggingface.co/onnx-community/depth-anything-v2-<size>/resolve/<revision>/onnx/model.onnx (revisions are listed in core/depth_anything.py).

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip model small Size of the network. small is fast and free for any use. base and large show finer detail. resolution 518 Long side (pixels) the network works at; both sides are rounded to a multiple of 14. 266 to 1036. Raise it for finer edges, lower it for speed. keep_model_loaded (optional) on Keep the Depth Anything model in VRAM between runs. Turn off to free its VRAM right after the run; ComfyUI's Free memory button does not reach this model.

Outputs: depth (MASK, 1 = nearest) and depth_preview (IMAGE, the depth as greyscale).

Licensing

small is Apache-2.0 and fine for commercial work. base and large are CC-BY-NC-4.0: non-commercial use only. Do not use them for paid jobs.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Depth is guessed, so thin objects (hair, wires) and glass can be wrong. Check depth_preview before blurring.
  • The map is relative per image. In a batch, each image is normalised on its own, so the same distance can get different values in two frames. For video this means the depth can flicker from frame to frame.
  • A close-up with no real background (a tight face crop) gives a depth map of the face shape itself, not of a "background".
  • You can soften depth edges with Mask Edge Smoother before using the map.
Under the hood

The image is resized (bicubic) so both sides are multiples of 14 with the long side close to resolution, then normalised with ImageNet mean and std and run through the ONNX model with onnxruntime directly (CUDA provider when available, otherwise CPU; one session is cached; with CUDA it uses the kSameAsRequested memory strategy, which keeps the extra GPU memory at about 0.4 to 0.5 GB instead of about 1.3 GB). The raw output is relative inverse depth; it is resized back to the image size (bilinear) and scaled per image to 0..1. A constant image gives all zeros. Images in a batch are processed one at a time. Source: core/depth_anything.py.

docs.title: Related nodes
docs.text:

docs.title: Depth Lens Blur
docs.text:
Fake a wide-aperture lens after the shot. The subject stays sharp and everything nearer or farther melts into smooth bokeh, according to a depth map.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → depth → Depth: Lens Blur Good for Background blur on portraits, product shots with creamy backgrounds, rescuing busy backgrounds Speed 2048 × 2048 image arriving from ComfyUI (CPU tensor), depth model excluded: about 0.03 s with a CUDA GPU (RTX 5090, transfers included); about 2 s on CPU only at max_blur 24, up to about 10 s at max_blur 96 with 16 layers

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
On a real lens, only one distance is sharp. The farther something is from that distance, the bigger its blur disc (the circle of confusion). This node does the same per pixel, using a depth map where 1 is nearest.

  • Focus (focus_depth) is the depth that stays sharp.
  • Depth of field (depth_of_field) is the width of the sharp zone. Small values act like f/1.4, large values like f/16.
  • Max blur (max_blur) is how big the blur gets at the farthest distance from focus, in pixels.

No depth map connected? The node estimates one itself with Depth Anything V2 (small model, 518 px). That needs onnxruntime (pip install onnxruntime-gpu).

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Depth: Lens Blur → Preview Image.
  2. Leave depth empty for automatic depth, or connect your own map (for example from Depth Anything V2).
  3. Try depth_of_field 0.1 and max_blur 24, then raise max_blur for stronger blur.
  4. To keep a person sharp automatically, connect a face mask to focus_mask (see below).

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip focus_depth 0.5 Depth value that stays sharp (1 = nearest). Ignored when focus_mask is connected. depth_of_field 0.1 Width of the sharp zone. 0 to 1. Lower = shallower focus. max_blur 24 Blur radius in pixels at the farthest distance from focus. 1 to 96. Scale up for large images. bokeh disc disc gives flat, lens-like bokeh. gaussian is a softer blur. disc for photographic look. layers 8 Number of blur steps blended together. 2 to 16. More = smoother transitions. blur_foreground on Off: only things behind the focus plane blur. Turn off to keep a near subject edge or foreground sharp. depth (optional) none Depth map, 1 = nearest. If missing, estimated internally. A map of another size is resized to the image. focus_mask (optional) none Subject mask. The median depth inside it becomes the focus. Works with face masks or SAM masks. keep_model_loaded (optional) on Keep the built-in Depth Anything model in VRAM between runs (only used when depth is not connected). Turn off to free its VRAM right after the run; ComfyUI's Free memory button does not reach this model.

Outputs: image (IMAGE) and coc (MASK, blur amount from 0 to 1; multiply by max_blur for pixels), useful for checking what gets blurred.

docs.title: Chaining: auto-focus on a face
docs.text: Face Detect Lite face_mask → Depth Lens Blur focus_mask. The face depth is measured automatically and the face stays sharp, however far the person stands. Any other mask works the same way, for example from SAM Mask.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• For video, the automatic depth is normalised on every frame, so the focus can flicker between frames. Feed a steady depth map, or a fixed focus_depth, for clips.
  • Check the depth map first. Blur follows the depth edges, so a wrong depth edge shows as a wrong blur edge.
  • Use max_blur in proportion to the image size: 24 is moderate on a 2K image, 60 or more suits 6K.
  • A little depth_of_field (0.05 to 0.15) keeps the whole face sharp, not just the eyes.
  • Add subtle noise or grain after the blur so blurred areas match the sharp ones.
Under the hood

Circle of confusion per pixel: clamp((|depth − focus| − dof/2) / (1 − dof/2), 0, 1) × max_blur. The node renders layers blur images with radii from 0 to max_blur and blends each pixel between the two nearest radii. Each layer is a normalised convolution (blur(image·w) / blur(w)) where w shrinks for pixels that are sharper than the layer, so a sharp foreground does not smear into the blurred background. Radii above 8 px are blurred on a downscaled copy and upsampled, so memory and time stay bounded (no unfold). The work runs on the GPU when one is available (ComfyUI passes images on the CPU; the result goes back to the same device). Peak GPU memory was about 0.45 GB at 2048 × 2048. The blur map is cleaned up with a small closing (window about max_blur / 8 px) so no thin sharp line appears where the depth crosses the focus plane between two blurred zones; wide in-focus areas stay untouched. NaN values in the depth or focus mask are treated as finite numbers, so one bad pixel cannot spoil the image. Limits: a blurred foreground does not spread over an in-focus background, and depth errors show up as blur errors. Source: core/depth_lens_blur.py.

docs.title: Dust & Spot Removal
docs.text:
Automatic dust-spot cleanup, like running the Spot Healing Brush over every speck at once. It only touches small spots and leaves eyes, hair and edges alone.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → filters → Filters: Dust & Spot Removal Good for Sensor dust on skies and backdrops, small specks on skin, scanned film dust, small blemishes

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Dust on the sensor shows up as small dark dots, most visible on smooth areas such as sky, studio backdrops and skin. This node looks for small spots that are darker (or brighter) than the area around them, then fills each one from the surrounding colour.

A spot only counts if it fits inside spot_size pixels. Bigger shapes such as eyes, moles you want to keep, and long thin things like hair strands are never touched.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Filters: Dust & Spot Removal → Preview Image.
  2. Keep mode on dark for sensor dust. Use bright for white specks, both for either.
  3. Set spot_size slightly bigger than the biggest speck you want gone.
  4. Look at the spot_mask output (with Mask Preview) to see what was removed. Raise or lower sensitivity until only the specks are selected.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip spot_size 12 Largest spot diameter in pixels (2 to 64). Anything bigger or longer is ignored. Keep it small on skin so freckles and pores stay. sensitivity 0.5 How faint a spot can be and still be caught (0 to 1). Higher catches fainter spots. Raise it slowly; too high starts to pick up skin texture. mode dark dark, bright or both. dark for sensor dust. mask (optional) none Spots are only removed where the mask is above 0.5. Use a skin or sky mask. protect_mask (optional) none Spots are never removed where this mask is above 0.5. Paint over freckles or beauty marks you want to keep. fill_mode (optional) blur blur = smooth fill from the surrounding colour (the original behaviour). texture = copies the best-matching nearby patch, so skin pores, film grain or fabric continue through the spot. Use texture on skin, grain or fabric where a smooth patch would look flat. About 2 s at 4K.

fill_mode was added in v1.8.0. The default blur keeps results identical to before. Detection is the same in both modes, so spot_mask is identical.

Outputs

Output What it is image The cleaned image. spot_mask White (1) where pixels were replaced, black (0) elsewhere. Everything outside it is unchanged.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• On portraits, connect a skin mask to mask (and the eyes and hair to protect_mask). The node already skips thin or elongated shapes and spots that sit in busy surroundings, so eyelashes, hair and edges are left alone, but a mask is still the safest way to keep real details such as moles or catchlights.
  • Check spot_mask first. If it shows long lines or lots of skin pores, lower sensitivity or spot_size.
  • Limit the node to the skin with mask, or protect the eyes and hair with protect_mask.
  • For heavier skin work, follow it with Skin Smoother or work on a separate layer with Frequency Separation.
  • Run it before sharpening, otherwise Smart Sharpen makes dust more visible.
  • Very big dust blobs (larger than 64 px) need manual cloning.
Under the hood

Luminance (Rec. 709 weights) is compared with a median background computed on a reduced-size copy (area average, then a 9 × 9 median in row chunks), so no big-kernel median ever runs at full resolution. The difference is thresholded (0.01 + 0.2 × (1 − sensitivity)²), then connected blobs are kept only if they are compact: bounding box at most spot_size pixels, aspect ratio at most 2, fill ratio at least 0.5 and at least about 3 px thick (a distance-transform peak of 1.3 px or more), so strands of hair and eyelashes are dropped. A blob must also sit in calm surroundings: the luminance spread in a window around it (with the blobs themselves left out) must stay below 0.25 × the spot contrast, which rejects spots on edges and in detail. On the clean sample portrait this changes about 0.006 % of the pixels. The blobs are dilated by max(1, spot_size // 6) pixels and limited by the masks. Filling uses normalised Gaussian convolution of the pixels outside the spots, computed at the reduced size and scaled back up, then blended in with a 1 px soft edge. A 2048 × 2048 image peaks at under 0.5 GB of GPU memory. If no spot is found the input is returned unchanged. With fill_mode set to texture, each spot is filled instead from the best-matching nearby patch, chosen by comparing the ring of pixels around the spot. The patch's brightness and colour are then matched to the surroundings. Source patches that contain a speck of their own are rejected, and where no clean patch fits, the spot falls back to the blur fill. Source: core/dust_spot.py.

docs.title: Edge-Aware Mask Refiner
docs.text:
Your mask is roughly right, but the edge cuts through the subject or leaves a halo. This node looks at the photo and pulls the mask edge onto the real boundary.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → mask → Mask: Edge-Aware Refiner Good for Fixing loose AI-segmentation masks, tightening a rough selection around a person or product, reducing halos

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Segmentation tools such as SAM often give a mask that is a few pixels off. A blur cannot fix that, because a blur does not know where the real edge is. This node uses the photo as a guide: where the photo has a strong edge, the mask edge snaps to it; where the photo is smooth, the mask stays smooth. This technique is called a guided filter.

It works best on edges with clear contrast between subject and background. For wispy hair where the edge is partly transparent, use Alpha Matte, which can recover real semi-transparency.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → your segmentation node → mask.
  2. Connect the mask to mask and the same photo to guide. The two must have the same width and height.
  3. Try radius 8 and eps 0.001. Increase radius if the mask is far off.
  4. Preview with Mask Preview in overlay mode with show_edges on.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip radius 8 How far (in pixels) the filter looks around each pixel. A larger radius can correct a looser mask. 1 to 32. Use roughly the size of the error you want to fix. eps 0.001 Edge sensitivity. Smaller values follow the photo's edges more tightly; larger values give a smoother, softer result. 0.000001 to 1. Try 0.0001 for crisp edges, 0.01 for soft ones. feather_sigma 0.0 Optional extra Gaussian blur after filtering, in pixels. 0 = off. 0 to 64. Use 1 to 3 for a gentle finish. guide_mode (optional) luma luma = follows the brightness of the guide (the original behaviour). rgb = follows the colour guide, so it also follows edges between colours of similar brightness. Try rgb for red hair on green leaves or similar colour-only edges.

Output: refined_mask (MASK).

Added in v1.8.0. The default luma gives exactly the same results as before, so existing workflows are unchanged.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Clean up the mask first with Mask Cleanup, then refine edges.
  • If the result looks too soft, lower eps. If it follows noise or texture, raise eps.
  • Do not use a huge radius on a mask that is already close. It can pull in unwanted background detail.
  • Run it before Mask Combine or compositing so every edge is already tight.
Under the hood

A grey-scale guided filter (He et al.) computed on the luma of the guide image (0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B). Window statistics come from box filters built from two 1-D average pools with replicate padding, so pixels at the image border are not pulled towards zero. The coefficients are a = cov(I, p) / (var(I) + eps) and b = mean(p) - a * mean(I); the output is the box-filtered a times the guide plus the box-filtered b, clamped to 0..1. An optional Gaussian blur follows. The guide must be float RGB with the same height and width as the mask; a guide batch of 1 is broadcast. With guide_mode set to rgb, the colour-guide form of the filter (He et al., 2010) is used instead: it uses the pack's own guided filter and works at any image size. Source: core/mask_edge_refine.py.

docs.title: Skin Smoother
docs.text:
Softens skin tone and small blemishes with an edge-preserving (bilateral) blur. Smooth areas get smoother, but strong edges such as eyelids, lips and hair lines stay crisp, so the face does not turn into plastic.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → filters → Edge-Aware Skin Smoother Good for Portrait skin cleanup, evening out tone, softening texture inside a skin mask

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A normal blur softens everything, including the edges you want to keep. A bilateral filter averages a pixel only with neighbours of a similar brightness and colour. Skin (similar values) gets averaged. An eye edge (very different values) does not.

Use strength to mix the smoothed result with the original, like lowering the opacity of a smoothing layer. Typical retouching doses are 0.3 to 0.5.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Edge-Aware Skin Smoother → Preview Image.
  2. Start with strength = 0.4, sigma_color = 0.1, sigma_space = 6.
  3. Turn tile_mode on for normal photo sizes (see the memory note below).
  4. Connect a skin MASK to mask to limit the effect to skin.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip strength 0.4 (0 to 1) Mix between original (0) and fully smoothed (1). 0.3 to 0.5 for natural skin. 0 returns the image unchanged. sigma_color 0.1 (0.01 to 0.5) How different two colours can be and still be averaged. On the 0 to 1 image scale, not 8-bit values. Small keeps more edges; large smooths across weak edges. sigma_space 6.0 (1 to 8) How far in pixels the smoothing reaches. Lower for small images. For wider smoothing, shrink the image first with a resize node. device auto auto uses CUDA if available, otherwise CPU. cuda fails if there is no CUDA. cpu forces CPU. tile_mode off Process the image in tiles to limit memory. See below. mask (optional) none Where smoothing applies: white = smoothed, black = original. A feathered skin mask avoids visible borders.

Output: image, the smoothed picture (IMAGE).

docs.title: Memory and tile_mode
docs.text:
The bilateral filter needs a lot of memory: roughly the number of pixels times the square of the kernel size.

  • Tile mode off: the node estimates the memory it needs. If that is above about 2 GB it stops with an error and suggests turning on tile_mode, lowering sigma_space or shrinking the image. At the default sigma_space = 6 the limit is only around 0.1 megapixel, so in practice you will want tile_mode on for real photos.
  • Tile mode on: the image is cut into tiles whose size is chosen so each tile fits in a memory budget of about 2 GB. Tiles are at most 512 px wide, and smaller when sigma_space is larger (at the default they come out around 120 px). Each tile includes a margin of neighbouring pixels, so you do not see seams.

The displayed hint on the tile_mode widget still mentions fixed 512 px tiles; the size is actually derived from the memory budget as described here.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Do less, twice, rather than once at full strength. Two passes at 0.3 look more natural than one at 0.8.
  • Combine with a skin mask and keep eyes, lips, brows and hair out of it. Skin Tone Tri-Region or the Mask nodes can help.
  • Add texture back afterwards with Smart Sharpen (luminance only), or use Frequency Separation first to smooth only the colour layer.
  • Check the effect with QA Image Diff to see where pixels changed.
Under the hood

Uses Kornia bilateral_blur with an L1 colour distance and replicate borders. The kernel size is 2 × ceil(3 × sigma_space) + 1. The result is strength × smoothed + (1 − strength) × original, then mixed with the original through the mask. If strength is 0, or the mask is all zeros, the input is returned untouched. Without tiling, the estimated allocation is B × C × H × W × kernel² × 4 bytes and anything above a budget of 2,000,000,000 bytes raises an error. With tiling, the tile side is the largest value that keeps a padded tile within that budget (with a safety factor for Kornia's temporaries), capped at 512 and never below 16. Source: core/smoother.py and nodes/smoother_node.py.

docs.title: Face Beauty Blend
docs.text:
Mixes a retouched picture back over the original, but only where your mask says so. It works like a layer with a mask and an opacity slider.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → face → Face Beauty Blend Good for The last step of a face chain; dialling an AI or smoothing pass down to taste; keeping eyes, lips and hair crisp

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A heavy retouch (AI skin, strong smoothing, frequency-separation fixes) often looks too much when applied everywhere at 100 %. Face Beauty Blend gives you the two controls you would use in an editor: a mask that decides where the retouch shows, and a strength that decides how much.

It works on whole pictures of the same size. If you pasted a face back with Unwrap Face, this node is the optional final polish.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect your original photo to base and the retouched version to retouched.
  2. Connect a mask to mask (white = show the retouch). A skin or face mask works well.
  3. Start with strength at 1.0 and feather at 8 to 16, then lower strength until it looks natural.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip base — The original photo. retouched — The edited version. Must be the same size as base. mask — Where the retouch shows (1 = fully, 0 = not at all). If its size differs from the image, it is resized to fit. strength 1.0 (0–1) Overall opacity of the retouch. Portrait skin passes often look best at about 0.5 to 0.8. feather 0 (0–64) Softens the mask edge, in pixels. 8 to 24 hides the transition. 0 keeps your mask as is.

Output: blended (IMAGE), the final picture.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Paint or generate the mask so it excludes eyes, brows, lips and hair. Those areas then stay sharp from the original.
  • To make the effect gentler without touching the mask, lower strength.
  • Need to soften or clean the mask first? Use Mask Cleanup or Mask Edge Smoother.
  • base and retouched must match in size and batch. A size mismatch raises an error.
Under the hood

The mask is clamped to [0, 1], resized bilinearly if needed, and blurred with a Gaussian of sigma feather / 3 (replicate border). Then blended = base × (1 − m) + retouched × m with m = blurred mask × strength. A mask batch of 1 is reused for every image in a batch. The code lives in core/face_pipeline.py (beauty_blend).

docs.title: Face Detect Lite
docs.text:
A quick face finder that runs on the GPU. It returns the same five key points as Face Detect, plus a ready-made mask of the face area.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → face → Face: Detect Lite (YuNet GPU) Good for Batches and quick previews; feeding Facial Aligner; limiting a later edit to the face area Speed About 31 ms on an RTX 5090 versus about 84 ms for MediaPipe on CPU (sample portrait)

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Use Lite when you want the face position fast and do not need the full 468-point mesh. It uses the YuNet network that ships with Kornia, so it works even if MediaPipe is not installed. It uses the GPU when one is available and falls back to CPU.

Stay with Face Detect and Face Landmarks when you need the dense mesh (warping, reshaping) or better handling of tilted and partly hidden faces.

Detect Lite (YuNet) Face Detect (MediaPipe) Needs MediaPipe No Yes conf in bbox_json Real detector score The threshold you set Face mask output Yes (face box) No Eye points Eye centres Outer eye corners Feeds the 468-point nodes No Use Face Landmarks

Both feed the aligner. The eye points differ by roughly 10–20 % of the eye distance, which does not matter for alignment.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect Load Image to Face: Detect Lite (YuNet GPU).
  2. Connect landmarks_json to the landmarks input of Facial Aligner. It reads the first face.
  3. Optional: use face_mask to limit a later edit to the face area.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip mode single_largest One largest face per image, or the top faces by box size. Portraits: keep the default. max_faces 1 (1–10) Faces per image in multi_top_k. Group shots: raise it. confidence_threshold 0.6 (0.1–0.95) Minimum detector score. Raise to drop false hits. nms_threshold 0.3 (0.1–0.9) Overlap above which duplicate boxes are merged. Lower it if you see duplicate boxes on one face. detect_size 640 (160–1024) Long side of the copy used for detection. Never enlarges. Keep 640 for portraits. Raise only for group shots with small faces.

Outputs:

Output Type Meaning landmarks_json STRING Per face: [L-eye, R-eye, nose-tip, L-mouth, R-mouth] in pixels. bbox_json STRING Per face: x, y, w, h (pixels), conf (real score) and batch_index. face_count INT Faces returned. face_mask MASK 1 inside the selected face boxes, 0 elsewhere.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• face_mask is a box, not a face outline. Feather it (for example with Mask Edge Smoother) before using it as an edit mask.
  • A larger detect_size is not always better. At very large values the detector can split or misplace big faces and add false hits on close-ups.
  • A pure black frame can trigger a false detection. Use a real image or a higher threshold.
  • Running a batch of portraits? Lite is the better pick: it is faster and needs no extra install.
Under the hood

The image is shrunk so its long side equals detect_size (smaller images are left alone), run through YuNet via kornia.contrib.FaceDetector, and boxes and points are scaled back to original pixels. Faces are sorted by box area. Images smaller than 64 px are padded with their mean colour for detection only. The detector is cached per device. Kornia downloads the weights once into the torch hub cache; if loading fails, the node raises a clear error. The code lives in core/face_detect_lite.py.

docs.title: Face Detect
docs.text:
Finds the face in your photo and reports where the eyes, nose and mouth corners are. It is the usual first step of any portrait edit that needs the face straightened or cropped.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → face → Face Detect (MediaPipe) Good for Feeding Facial Aligner; picking the biggest face in a group shot; counting faces Speed About 84 ms on CPU for the sample portrait (MediaPipe, desktop CPU)

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Most face edits (an AI skin pass, a face swap, a detail enhance) work best on a face that is upright, centred and at a fixed size. To get there, the pack first needs to know where the face is. Face Detect answers with five points per face: left eye, right eye, nose tip, left mouth corner and right mouth corner. A landmark is simply a named point on the face.

Choose this node when you already use MediaPipe in your setup, or when you also plan to use Face Landmarks and want both to agree on the same face. If you only need fast detection and a face mask, try Face Detect Lite.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Add Load Image and connect IMAGE to Face Detect (MediaPipe).
  2. Leave mode on single_largest for a normal portrait.
  3. Connect landmarks_json to the landmarks input of Facial Aligner.
  4. For a group photo, switch mode to multi_top_k and raise max_faces.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip mode single_largest single_largest returns the face with the biggest box. multi_top_k returns up to max_faces faces, biggest first. Portraits: keep the default. max_faces 1 (1–10) Upper limit on returned faces. Ignored in single_largest. Crowd scenes: 5–10. confidence_threshold 0.5 (0.1–0.95) How sure MediaPipe must be before a face counts. Above about 0.85 it can miss normal portraits. Lower it if a face is missed.

Outputs:

Output Type Meaning landmarks_json STRING JSON list, one entry per face, in the order [L-eye, R-eye, nose-tip, L-mouth, R-mouth] (pixel [x, y]). bbox_json STRING JSON list of face boxes and extra info per face. face_count INT Number of faces returned.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• For a single-subject portrait, single_largest is the safe choice: it ignores a stray face in the background.
  • The conf value in bbox_json is the threshold you set, not a per-face score. To rank faces, use box size (multi_top_k already sorts by it).
  • No face found? Lower confidence_threshold, or check that the face is not tiny or heavily turned away.
  • Edits that need the full face mesh (reshaping, warping) use Face Landmarks instead. This node only gives five points.
Under the hood

The node wraps the MediaPipe FaceLandmarker (tasks API). The model file face_landmarker.task (about 5 MB) is downloaded once into ComfyUI/models/mediapipe/ the first time the node runs. The five points are taken from the 468-point mesh, so the eye points sit on the outer eye corners. The detector object is cached between runs. If mediapipe is missing, the node raises an error that tells you to install it. The code lives in core/face_detect.py.

docs.title: Face Landmarks
docs.text:
Maps the face with 468 points (eyes, brows, nose, lips, jawline, cheeks). Those points are what the warp nodes use to reshape a face.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → face → Face Landmarks (MediaPipe 468) Good for Feeding Face Warp or Face Warp TPS; checking how well the mesh fits a face

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Five points are enough to straighten a face, but not to reshape one. To slim a jaw, lift an eye or copy an expression from another photo, you need a dense map. A landmark is a numbered point on the face, and the same number always sits on the same spot (for example the tip of the nose), so you can compare a face in two photos point by point.

Run the node once on your photo for the "source" points, and once on a reference or edited version for the "destination" points. Feed both into a warp node.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect Load Image to Face Landmarks (MediaPipe 468).
  2. Leave draw_overlay on and look at overlay in a Preview Image to confirm the dots sit on the face.
  3. Connect landmarks to src_landmarks of Face Warp TPS (or Face Warp).
  4. Get dst_landmarks from a second Face Landmarks node run on the target picture.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip max_num_faces 1 (1–10) Most faces to find per image. Missing faces are filled with NaN (no data). Keep 1 for portraits. The warp nodes use the first face. min_detection_confidence 0.5 (0.0–1.0) How sure MediaPipe must be before a face counts. Lower it if a real face is missed. refine_landmarks on Kept for compatibility. The dense 468-point output is always used. Leave as is. draw_overlay on Draws the points as green dots on the overlay image. Turn off if you do not need the preview.

Outputs:

Output Type Meaning landmarks LANDMARKS The 468 points per face, in normalised [0, 1] image coordinates. Connect only to nodes that take LANDMARKS. overlay IMAGE Your photo with the points drawn on.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• LANDMARKS is a special type. It does not connect to landmarks_json of Facial Aligner; use a face detect node for that.
  • Run the node on the same resolution as the image you will warp, or at least the same framing, so points line up.
  • If a face is not found, its slot holds NaN. Warp nodes then return the image unchanged.
  • Detection noise is real: two runs on slightly different crops disagree by a few pixels. For this reason Face Warp TPS has a smoothness setting.
Under the hood

The node uses the MediaPipe FaceLandmarker (tasks API) and shares its model file with Face Detect. The result is a (batch, faces, 468, 2) float tensor, NaN-padded when fewer faces are found. The image is converted to 8-bit RGB for MediaPipe. The code lives in core/face_pipeline.py.

docs.title: Face Warp TPS
docs.text:
Moves the face from source landmarks to destination landmarks with a single smooth, rubber-sheet style distortion. Use it for subtle reshaping where triangle seams or kinks would show.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → face → Face Warp (TPS smooth) Good for Slimming, eye or jaw adjustments; matching a face to another photo; edits that must look natural Speed About 19 ms on CUDA and about 0.85 s on CPU for a 1536×2048 image with 468 points (RTX 5090 / desktop CPU)

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A thin-plate spline (TPS) is a smooth surface that bends like a thin metal plate: it passes through your control points and stays as flat as possible between them. Applied to an image, it gives one continuous distortion with no visible triangle edges.

Pick TPS for gentle, natural changes and when you want GPU speed. Pick Face Warp (Delaunay) when the change must stay strictly inside the face mesh or when every one of the 468 points must be honoured locally.

Delaunay (Face Warp) TPS (this node) Field One affine patch per triangle One smooth global field Seams or kinks Possible on triangle edges for large moves None Outside the face Unchanged Fades out smoothly (pinned by anchor_border) Runs on CPU (OpenCV) GPU when available

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Run Face Landmarks on your photo and connect landmarks to src_landmarks.
  2. Run Face Landmarks on the target (a second photo, or a zoomed copy) and connect it to dst_landmarks.
  3. Keep the defaults and check warped in a Preview Image.
  4. If you still see ripples, raise smoothness.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip max_points 468 (16–468) Most landmark pairs used for the warp. Pairs that move are always kept. Keep 468. Lower only for speed, since fewer pins let nearby features drift. anchor_border on Pins points along the image border so the background does not swim. Turn off only if the whole frame should move with the face (pure shift or scale). smoothness 1.0 (0–20) 0 lands every landmark exactly. Higher values absorb detection noise. Use 0 for hand-edited points. Keep 1 or more when targets come from another photo. Raise it if ripples remain.

Output: warped (IMAGE), the reshaped picture.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Landmarks from a second detection differ from the source by detector noise as well as the real shape change. On the sample portrait that noise is about 13–17 px (median) for a 3–6 % zoomed copy. Matching it exactly would fold the image, so keep smoothness at 1 or higher for such targets.
  • Move groups of neighbouring landmarks together. Pulling a few isolated points creates wide, rubbery effects.
  • Missing faces (NaN points) or fewer than 3 valid pairs return the image unchanged.
  • Warp first, then run skin retouch, so texture work follows the final shape.
Under the hood

The spline (kernel r² log r plus an affine part) is fitted on the output-to-input mapping, so every output pixel samples the source where the spline points. It is evaluated exactly on a grid with a 4 px step, upsampled bicubically to full size, then used to resample the image bilinearly. With smoothness = 0, control points land within about 0.6 px of their destination on a real 1536×2048 portrait. Moved pairs (more than 0.5 px) are never dropped when max_points is lowered; the rest is filled half with the unmoved pairs nearest the edit and half with evenly spaced ones. With anchor_border on, extra pairs with identical source and destination (corners plus 3 per edge) pin the border; higher smoothness relaxes them slightly (well under 1 px at the default). Peak memory is about 480 MiB at that size, mostly image buffers. The code lives in core/face_warp_tps.py.

docs.title: Face Warp
docs.text:
Moves the face from one set of landmarks to another, like a precise liquify driven by the face mesh. The result stays strictly inside the mesh, which keeps the background untouched.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → face → Face Warp (Delaunay per-triangle) Good for Controlled face-shape changes; matching a face to another photo's shape; edits that must not leak outside the face

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
The node cuts the face into small triangles from the source landmarks (a Delaunay triangulation) and stretches each triangle to its new position. Every one of the 468 points is honoured locally.

Choose it when the change should stay confined to the face mesh. Choose Face Warp TPS instead for gentle, natural deformations where a triangle edge or kink would show. The Face category overview compares them side by side.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Run Face Landmarks on your photo and connect landmarks to src_landmarks.
  2. Get dst_landmarks from a second Face Landmarks on the target picture (or an edited set of points).
  3. Connect your image and check warped in a Preview Image.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
The node has no widgets, only inputs.

Input Type What it does image IMAGE The photo to reshape. src_landmarks LANDMARKS Where the features are now. dst_landmarks LANDMARKS Where they should end up. Output Type Meaning warped IMAGE The reshaped image.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Source and destination must come from the same layout (both 468-point). The node uses the first face of each.
  • If a face is missing on either side, the image comes back unchanged.
  • Big moves can show seams along triangle edges. Use Face Warp TPS for a smoother field.
  • Warp first, retouch skin after, so texture work lands on the final shape.
Under the hood

Landmarks are read as normalised [0, 1] or pixel coordinates. Points that are not finite are dropped, and fewer than 3 valid pairs returns the image unchanged. SciPy builds the Delaunay triangulation on the source points, then OpenCV warps each triangle with an affine transform and composites it with anti-aliased edges. This runs on the CPU. The code lives in core/face_pipeline.py.

docs.title: Facial Aligner
docs.text:
Straightens and crops a face into a standard square frame (the same layout used by face datasets such as FFHQ), using five landmark points. It also gives you the matrix needed to paste the edited face back later.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → geometry → Landmark Facial Aligner Good for Preparing a face for AI face editing, upscaling or inpainting; consistent face crops for batches

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Face models work best when the eyes, nose and mouth are always in the same place. This node rotates the picture so the eyes are level, scales it so the face has a fixed size, and crops a square. Hair and chin room is controlled by padding.

It is the first half of a round trip: align the face, edit the crop, then return it to the original photo with Unwrap Face using inverse_matrix_json.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Face Detect Lite (or Face Detect).
  2. Connect its landmarks_json output to the landmarks input of Landmark Facial Aligner.
  3. Choose target_size (1024 is a good start) and padding = 0.2.
  4. Send image_aligned to Preview Image.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Setting Default What it does Tip image — The portrait to align. landmarks sample text for the sample portrait Five points as JSON: left eye, right eye, nose, left mouth corner, right mouth corner. Pixel values or 0 to 1 values both work. Connect it from a face-detection node instead of typing. target_size 1024 Side of the square output: 512, 768 or 1024. Smaller is faster; 1024 suits SDXL. padding 0.2 (0 to 0.5) Space kept around the face. 0 is a tight crop, higher values show more hair and chin. 0.2 to 0.3 for most portraits. Output Type Meaning image_aligned IMAGE The aligned square face crop. inverse_matrix_json STRING The matrix that maps the crop back onto the original photo. Feed it to Unwrap Face.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Values of 1.5 or less are treated as 0 to 1 coordinates; larger values are treated as pixels.
  • Use a wide-angle correction first (Lens Distortion) if the face is near the edge of a wide shot; stretched faces give less accurate landmarks.
  • For a batch, give one set of landmarks per image (a list of five-point lists). One set is reused for every image.
Under the hood

The five points are matched to a canonical layout with a similarity transform (rotation, uniform scale, shift; Umeyama method), then applied with Kornia warp_affine to a target_size × target_size output. The inverse is returned as a 3×3 matrix. Landmarks must be non-negative; the node raises an error if they fall outside the image after normalisation. Only 512, 768 and 1024 are accepted for target_size. Source: core/facial_aligner.py and nodes/facial_aligner_node.py.

docs.title: Frequency Recombine
docs.text:
Rebuilds a picture from the two layers made by Frequency Separation. Edit colour on low, texture on high, then put them back. One slider lets you push pores and fine detail up or down at the same time.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → filters → Frequency Recombine (low + high) Good for Finishing a frequency-separation retouch, boosting or softening skin texture without touching colour

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Frequency Separation splits a photo into a smooth low layer (colour and light) and a signed high layer (texture). The high layer holds negative values, so ordinary blend or add nodes cannot join the two again: they clamp the negative half away. Frequency Recombine adds them correctly and only clamps the final picture to the 0 to 1 range.

The detail setting scales the texture layer before it is added back:

  • 1.0 returns the original exactly if you did not edit either layer.
  • Above 1.0 boosts texture: pores, hair and fabric get stronger.
  • Below 1.0 softens texture. 0.0 gives you the low layer alone.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Frequency Separation.
  2. Connect low and high to the same-named inputs of Frequency Recombine.
  3. Leave detail = 1.0 and preview: you should see your original photo.
  4. Edit low (for example with Skin Smoother), then try detail = 1.2 to 1.6 for more texture.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Setting Default What it does Tip low — The colour-and-tone layer, edited or not. From Frequency Separation. high — The texture layer. Signed values. Connect it directly. Do not pass it through a node that clamps. detail 1.0 (0 to 3, step 0.05) How much texture to add back. 0.8 to 1.0 for softer skin, 1.2 to 1.6 for stronger texture. Output Type Meaning image IMAGE low + detail × high, clamped to 0..1.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Check the round trip first: with no edits and detail = 1.0 the result should match the original.
  • Smooth low and keep detail at or slightly above 1 to hide blotches but keep pores.
  • Keep radius in Frequency Separation the same for the whole job. The two layers only match if they come from the same split.
  • A large detail on a noisy photo also boosts the noise. Try smaller steps.
  • Both layers must have the same width and height.
Under the hood

The result is low + detail × high in float32, clamped once at the end. Both inputs must be RGB with the same height and width. Batch sizes must match, or one side must be 1 (it broadcasts). detail outside 0..3 raises an error. Source: frequency_recombine in core/frequency.py and the wrapper in nodes/frequency_node.py.

docs.title: Frequency Separation
docs.text:
Splits an image into two layers: low (soft colour, light and shadow) and high (fine detail such as pores, hair and fabric texture). You can then fix blotchy skin tone on one layer without touching texture on the other.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → filters → GPU Frequency Separation Good for Skin retouching, removing colour blotches while keeping pores, texture-only sharpening or softening

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Frequency separation is the classic portrait-retouching technique:

  • Low frequencies are the big, slow changes: skin colour, shading, make-up tone. This is the image blurred with a Gaussian filter.
  • High frequencies are the small, fast changes: pores, stubble, eyelashes, fabric weave. This is everything the blur removed.

Retouch colour problems on low, texture problems on high, then put the two back together. A larger radius moves more of the picture into high.

docs.title: Why high can be negative
docs.text:
high is the original minus the blurred copy. Where a pixel is brighter than its surroundings (a bright pore edge, a hair highlight) the result is positive. Where it is darker (a pore, a shadow in a crease) the result is negative. On average the values sit around zero. An image can only store values from 0 to 1, so a negative value cannot be shown as a normal picture: the preview looks dark or oddly coloured. That is expected. The pieces still add up exactly: low + high = original.

Rebuilding the image

Use Frequency Recombine to put the layers back together. Blend nodes that clamp values to 0..1 (including the layer nodes in this pack) throw the negative half of high away, so the sum no longer matches the original.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → GPU Frequency Separation.
  2. Leave radius = 8, sigma = 0, precision = float32.
  3. Send low to Preview Image to see the smooth layer. The high preview looks dark; that is normal.
  4. Edit low or high with your own nodes, then join them with Frequency Recombine. At detail = 1 it restores the original exactly.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Setting Default What it does Tip radius 8 (1 to 128) Size of the blur in pixels. Detail smaller than this goes to high. Small (3 to 6) for fine texture, larger for bigger blotches. Must be at most half of the shorter image side. sigma 0.0 (0 to 50) Blur softness. 0 means automatic: radius / 2. Leave at 0 unless you need to match another tool. precision float32 float32 rebuilds the original almost exactly. float16 is about twice as fast on a modern GPU with a rebuild error around 0.001. Use float32 for final work. Output Type Meaning low IMAGE The blurred, smooth layer. high IMAGE The detail layer. Can contain negative values.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Pick radius relative to image size. The same 8 px is fine detail on a 1 MP image and almost nothing on a 24 MP image.
  • Smooth skin tone on low with Skin Smoother; leave high alone so pores survive.
  • Use Detail Mask when you need to protect textured areas.
  • Avoid float16 on CPU. It can be slow and less precise there.
Under the hood

low is a Kornia gaussian_blur2d with kernel size 2 × radius + 1, sigma radius / 2 unless overridden, and replicate borders. high = working − low in the chosen precision. Input must be 3-channel RGB in 0..1; radius above half the shorter side raises an error. A sigma larger than radius / 2 logs a warning because the kernel truncates the tail of the Gaussian. Source: core/frequency.py and nodes/frequency_node.py.

docs.title: HALD Identity
docs.text:
Creates a special image that contains every colour in a grid and does nothing on its own. Whatever grade you apply to it can be saved as a .cube LUT.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → HALD Identity Good for Starting a LUT export, turning any colour-only node chain into a reusable look Speed Instant. Higher levels make a bigger image (level 12 is 1728 × 1728 px)

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Think of it as a blank colour chart. It looks like a smooth, multicoloured pattern. If you send it through colour nodes (tone curve, colour balance, …), the pattern changes in exactly the way those nodes change every colour in a photo. LUT Export then reads the graded chart and writes the grade out as a .cube file.

This is the first step of the LUT workflow:

HALD Identity → colour nodes only → LUT Export → .cube file

Colour-only nodes between HALD and Export

The chart only survives colour operations that treat each pixel on its own, such as Tone Curve or Hue/Saturation per Range. Do not blur, sharpen, resize, crop, rotate or add grain: they move or mix the pixels and the exported LUT will be wrong.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Add HALD Identity and leave level at 8.
  2. Connect its image output to your grade (for example Tone Curve).
  3. Connect the graded image to LUT Export and wire level from HALD Identity to LUT Export's level input.

The full walk-through is on the LUT Export page.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip level 8 Quality of the LUT. Choices: 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. 8 gives a 64-point cube, the usual standard for creative looks. Level LUT grid Chart size 4 16 points per side 64 × 64 px 8 64 points per side 512 × 512 px 12 144 points per side 1728 × 1728 px

Outputs:

  • image — the identity chart, a single image.
  • level — the same number as an integer, so you can wire it straight into LUT Export.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Stay at 8 unless you have a reason. Higher levels give a smoother LUT for extreme grades but make a larger file and use more memory.
  • Always wire level to LUT Export. A mismatch raises an error.
  • Preview the chart before the grade, then again after, to check it still looks like a smooth colour pattern.
Under the hood

For level L the LUT has N = L² points per axis and the chart is L³ × L³ pixels, following the ImageMagick HALD convention. Red varies fastest along x, green along y, and blue steps through the L × L tiles. The tensor is float32 in [0, 1], shape (1, L³, L³, 3). The node offers levels 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12; the underlying function accepts 2 to 16.

docs.title: Related nodes
docs.text:
• LUT Export — writes the graded chart to a .cube.
  • LUT Import — applies a .cube to a photo.
  • Tone Curve — a common grade to put between the two.
  • Tone Match LUT — builds a LUT automatically from a reference image.

docs.text: LUT Export example workflow. HALD Identity, Tone Curve and LUT Export in a row; a Preview Any node shows the written file path. No input image is needed.

docs.title: HDR Merge
docs.text:
Give it a bracket of the same scene, such as dark, normal and bright. It returns one photo with the best-exposed parts of each shot.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Color: HDR Merge (bracket) Good for Interiors with bright windows, landscapes with a bright sky, real estate, any high-contrast scene shot as a bracket Speed About 1 s for three 2 MP frames, on the CPU

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A single exposure often cannot hold both a bright window and a dark room. A bracket (for example -2, 0 and +2 EV) captures both. This node picks, pixel by pixel, the well-exposed, contrasty and colourful parts of each frame and blends them smoothly.

The method is exposure fusion. It needs no exposure values and no camera response curve, and the result is ready to view. There is no tone-mapping step with sliders to tune.

The result is a normal display-ready image, not a 32-bit HDR file. Treat it as a starting point and finish it with Auto Tone or ColorLab.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load the bracketed photos and combine them into one batch with Batch Images (or Load Image Batch). The order does not matter, and all frames must be the same size.
  2. Connect the batch to Color: HDR Merge (bracket) and add a Preview Image.
  3. Keep align and deghost on.
  4. Finish with Auto Tone or ColorLab if you want to adjust the look.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip images A batch of 2 or more bracketed shots, in any order, all the same size. Use Batch Images or Load Image Batch to build the batch. align on Lines up hand-held shots by fixing small shifts (translation only). Turn off for shots taken on a tripod, if you want the fastest result. deghost on Where something moved between shots (people, leaves), uses the middle exposure, brightness-matched, so nothing appears twice. Turn off for fully static scenes.

Output

Output What it is image One merged image.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Shoot -2, 0 and +2 EV on a tripod, or use a fast burst, so the frames match as closely as possible.
  • Big movements or rotation between shots are not aligned. Reshoot, or fix the rotation first with Auto Align if the frames allow it.
  • Moving subjects such as people, cars and tree branches are handled by deghost. Check them at 100 % after merging.
  • The merge looks natural and slightly flat. Add contrast and colour afterwards with Auto Tone, ColorLab or Shadows/Highlights Pro.
  • Two frames also work, but three or more give smoother transitions.
Under the hood

Frames are sorted by brightness and the middle one is the reference. With align, each frame is shifted onto the reference with median-threshold-bitmap alignment (OpenCV AlignMTB). A shift larger than 5 % of the long edge is treated as a failed alignment and ignored.

With deghost, each frame is first scaled to the reference brightness. Where it still disagrees strongly, which means movement, the frame takes the brightness-matched reference pixels with a soft edge.

The frames are fused with Mertens exposure fusion (Mertens, Kautz and Van Reeth, 2007): a multi-resolution blend weighted by contrast, saturation and well-exposedness. It runs on the CPU in OpenCV. Source: core/hdr_merge.py, wrapper nodes/hdr_merge_node.py.

docs.text:

  • ColorLab: full colour and tone control
  • Shadows/Highlights Pro: recover shadows and highlights further
  • Auto Align: align frames that are rotated or shifted a lot

docs.title: Heal / Content-Aware Fill
docs.text:
Paint a mask over something you want gone, such as a wire, a blemish, a logo or a stray object. The node fills the hole with texture and structure taken from nearby, like Content-Aware Fill in Photoshop.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → filters → Filters: Heal / Content-Aware Fill Good for Wires and poles, skin marks and scars, small objects on grass, sky or walls, logos on flat surfaces Speed On a GPU, 1 to 3 s for typical masks on an 8 MP photo, under 1.1 GB VRAM at 4K. On a CPU it is much slower: about 25 s for a 400 px hole at 4K.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A clone stamp copies one patch by hand. This node does the search for you: for every pixel inside the hole it looks for the most similar patches in the area around it, then blends them so grain, pores and grass blades continue into the filled area.

It works best on texture: skin, sky, grass, sand, walls. Complex structure is harder. Arches, text and faces can come out broken. For those, mask generously and try a larger context, or retouch by hand afterwards.

Mask parts that are far apart are healed separately, so scattered spots are fine. The result is the same every time you run it.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image and a mask (paint it in the Mask Editor, or build one with other mask nodes). White means remove and fill.
  2. Connect both to Filters: Heal / Content-Aware Fill and add a Preview Image.
  3. Keep mode on content_aware. Use smooth only on flat, textureless areas.
  4. If the fill looks wrong, make the mask a bit larger, or raise context to 2.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image The photo to retouch. mask White = remove and fill. Cover the object and its shadow or halo. mode content_aware content_aware rebuilds texture and structure from nearby patches. smooth is a soft colour fill with no texture. smooth is for flat areas such as a clean sky or studio backdrop. grow 2 0 to 64 px. Adds this many pixels around the mask. Raise it to catch halos and soft shadows. feather 1.5 0 to 32 px. Soft blend outside the mask edge. Raise it on smooth gradients. Keep it low on detailed texture. context (optional) 1.0 0.25 to 8. How far around each mask part to search, as a multiple of its size. Raise it when the right texture is far away from the hole.

Output

Output What it is image The photo with the masked area filled.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Mask a little too much rather than too little. Leftover edges of the object are the most common reason a fill looks wrong.
  • For a long wire across the sky, a thin mask with grow 3 to 6 is usually enough.
  • Several separate marks in one mask are fine. Each part is healed on its own, with its own search area.
  • If a fill repeats an unwanted pattern, lower context so the search stays near the hole. If it lacks the right texture, raise it.
  • For freckles or pimples on a face, Auto Blemish finds them for you. To remove sensor dust, use Dust & Spot Removal.
Under the hood

content_aware is exemplar-based completion (Wexler, Shechtman and Irani, 2007) with a parallel PatchMatch search. The hole is filled from coarse to fine over an image pyramid. At each level, every pixel whose 7x7 patch touches the hole looks for the most similar fully known patch nearby. Each hole pixel then becomes a weighted vote of the overlapping source patches.

Only the area around each mask part (its bounding box plus a margin set by context) is processed, and memory grows with that area only. The feather band is filled too and blended from opaque at the mask edge to the original at its outer edge. The search uses a fixed random seed, so results repeat exactly.

smooth fills by normalised convolution of the surrounding colours. Source: core/heal.py, wrapper nodes/heal_node.py.

docs.text:

  • Dust & Spot Removal: finds sensor dust and small spots by itself
  • Mask Morphology: grow, shrink or clean your mask first
  • Mask Preview: check what the mask covers

docs.title: Detail Mask
docs.text:
Finds where your photo has fine detail (eyelashes, hair, fabric weave, edges) and returns it as a mask. Use it to sharpen only where there is texture, or to keep smoothing away from detail.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → mask → High-Frequency Detail Masker Good for Sharpening only textured areas, protecting detail during skin smoothing, building a mask for noise or grain work

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
In frequency terms, high-frequency content is the fine, fast-changing part of a photo: pores, hair strands, edges. Low-frequency content is the smooth colour and tone. This node measures how much fine detail each pixel has, then keeps the top share of the strongest pixels.

Typical uses:

  • Gate Smart Sharpen so flat skin and sky do not get sharpened.
  • Protect eyes, lashes and hair when you run Skin Smoother.
  • Invert it to get the smooth areas only.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect your photo to image.
  2. Start with kernel_type laplacian and sensitivity 0.4.
  3. Preview the mask with Mask Preview. Raise sensitivity to include more.
  4. Use the mask as the gate in your sharpen or smooth step.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip kernel_type laplacian How detail is measured. laplacian finds fine detail in all directions; sobel favours edges; fs_gaussian uses the difference between the photo and a light blur (the high-pass of frequency separation). Start with laplacian. sensitivity 0.5 Share of pixels kept as detail. 0 gives an empty mask, 1 gives a full mask. 0 to 1. For portraits, 0.3 to 0.6 is typical. threshold_mode relative_percentile relative_percentile adapts to each image, so the same sensitivity selects a similar share of pixels. absolute is scaled by the strongest detail in the image. Use the default. absolute can be thrown off by one bright speck. mask (optional) none Limits the result to a region. The output is multiplied by it. Use a face or subject mask.

Output: mask_detail (MASK), values 0 or 1.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• The output is a hard on/off mask. Soften it with Mask Edge Smoother or a blur before using it as a blend mask.
  • Detail is measured on the average of the colour channels (grey), so colour-only edges are weak.
  • Noisy photos look "full of detail". Denoise first if the mask lights up on grain.
  • sensitivity is a share of the image, not a strength. A flat photo still returns the requested share, just on its relatively sharpest parts.
Under the hood

Luma is the mean of the RGB channels. High-pass options: laplacian (Kornia, 3x3, replicate border), sobel (Kornia, normalised gradient magnitude) or fs_gaussian (luma minus a 5x5, sigma 1 Gaussian blur). In relative_percentile mode the threshold is the per-image k-th value of the absolute high-pass so that about sensitivity of the pixels pass. In absolute mode the high-pass is divided by its per-image maximum and compared with 1 - sensitivity. Sensitivity 0 and 1 are shortcuts for an empty or full mask. Source: core/detail_masker.py.

docs.title: Related nodes
docs.text:
• Smart Sharpen to sharpen through this mask
  • Skin Smoother to smooth around the protected detail
  • Frequency Separation for the low/high split behind fs_gaussian
  • Mask Preview for viewing the result
