docs.title: Hue/Saturation per Range
docs.text:
Picks one colour on the hue wheel and changes only that colour: turn greens a little more yellow, mute a loud red, or make the blues deeper.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Hue/Saturation per Range Good for Calming a colour that is too loud, fixing foliage or sky colour, shifting a product colour, selective desaturation

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
This is the selective-colour move from a photo editor's Hue/Saturation panel. You choose a centre colour in degrees on the hue wheel and a band width. Pixels near that hue are affected most; the effect fades smoothly to nothing at the band's edge, and grey pixels are left alone. Colours outside the band do not move at all, and brightness is never changed.

Hue wheel positions: 0 red, 60 yellow, 120 green, 180 cyan, 240 blue, 300 magenta.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Hue/Saturation per Range → Preview Image.
  2. Set hue_center to the colour you want to change (for example 120 for green) and band_width to about 30.
  3. Move hue_shift or sat_mult and watch only that colour respond.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image required The picture to adjust. hue_center 0 (0 to 360) The colour to target, in degrees on the hue wheel. 0 red, 60 yellow, 120 green, 180 cyan, 240 blue, 300 magenta. band_width 30 (0 to 180) Half-width of the band in degrees. Full effect at the centre, fading to none at this distance. 30 narrow, 60 medium, 180 the whole wheel. hue_shift 0 (-180 to 180) Rotates the hue inside the band, in degrees. Small values (5 to 20) look natural. sat_mult 1.0 (0 to 2) Multiplies saturation inside the band. 1 is unchanged, 0 removes colour, 2 doubles it. 0.6 to calm a loud colour. sat_add 0 (-1 to 1) Adds or subtracts saturation after the multiplication. Useful to colour up pale areas.

Output: image, the adjusted picture.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Widen band_width to 45 to 60 for natural-looking results; very narrow bands can leave visible edges in smooth gradients.
  • To calm red patches in skin, target 0 to 10 with a gentle sat_mult of about 0.8.
  • To push a sky deeper without touching skin, target 220 to 240 and raise sat_mult.
  • For several colours, chain more than one Hue/Saturation per Range. For a full panel with eight bands, see ColorLab.
  • Use Saturation Mask to protect already-strong colours from further boosting.
Under the hood

The image goes to HSV (Kornia). A band mask is built from the circular hue distance to hue_center: it is 1 at the centre and falls linearly to 0 at band_width; pixels with no saturation get 0. Hue is rotated by hue_shift × mask, saturation becomes s × (1 + (sat_mult − 1) × mask) + sat_add × mask clamped to 0..1, value is unchanged, and the result is blended with the input by the same mask. With band_width = 0 only pixels exactly at the centre hue are selected.

docs.text:

  • Saturation Mask: build masks from colour strength
  • Color Matcher: match overall colour to a reference
  • Luminosity Masking: limit the change to shadows, midtones or highlights

docs.title: Layer Add
docs.text:
Adds one layer to a layer stack, the way you would drop a new layer into Photoshop: pick a blend mode, set opacity and fill, optionally add a mask, and optionally clip it to the layer below.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → compositing → Compositing: Layer Add Good for Colour grades, light leaks, dodge-and-burn layers, texture overlays, local tints through a mask

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Use it for finishing composites that should be repeatable and adjustable. Each Layer Add node is one layer. Chain several to build a stack from bottom to top: the first one you add sits directly above the background, the next one above that, and so on.

How the stack works:

  1. Layer Stack Start creates the background layer.
  2. Layer Add appends layers on top, each with its own blend mode, opacity, fill, mask and clipping.
  3. Layer Group can nest a whole sub-stack as a single layer.
  4. Layer Flatten merges everything into one image.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Layer Stack Start.
  2. Stack output → Layer Add stack. Plug the image you want on top into layer_image.
  3. Try blend_mode = soft_light and opacity = 0.5.
  4. Add more Layer Add nodes if you need them, then finish with Layer Flatten → Preview Image.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip stack — The stack to add to. From Layer Stack Start or another Layer Add. layer_image — The image to place on top. Resized to the background size if it differs. blend_mode normal How this layer mixes with everything below it. See the list below. opacity 1.0 (0 to 1) Overall strength of the layer. Start at 0.3 to 0.6 for grades. fill 1.0 (0 to 1) A second strength control. Multiplies with opacity. clip_to_below off Limits the layer to the mask of the layer directly below. Only has an effect if that layer has a layer_mask. layer_mask (optional) none Where the layer shows: white = fully, black = not at all. Resized to the canvas if needed.

Output: LAYER_STACK, the stack with your new layer on top.

docs.title: Blend modes
docs.text:
All 27 modes in core/blend_modes.py, grouped like the Photoshop menu:

Group Modes Normal normal, dissolve Darken darken, multiply, color_burn, linear_burn, darker_color Lighten lighten, screen, color_dodge, linear_dodge, lighter_color Contrast overlay, soft_light, hard_light, vivid_light, linear_light, pin_light, hard_mix Comparative difference, exclusion, subtract, divide Colour hue, saturation, color, luminosity

dissolve works like Photoshop: each pixel becomes either fully the layer or fully the base, with a chance equal to opacity × fill × mask. It does not blend colours. The pattern uses a fixed seed, so the same settings always give the same result.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Soft Light or Overlay at low opacity is the quickest way to add contrast or a colour wash without clipping.
  • Multiply darkens, Screen lightens: use them with a blurred mask for dodge-and-burn style work.
  • Color applies only the hue and saturation of the layer, which is handy for tinting skin without changing brightness. Luminosity does the opposite.
  • Feed a mask from the Mask nodes (for example Luminosity Masking) into layer_mask to limit a grade to the highlights or shadows.
  • Use clip_to_below to keep a layer inside the masked area of the layer under it.
Under the hood

Layers are rendered in order. The blend result is computed from the running image and the layer image (both clamped to 0..1), then mixed back with lerp using alpha = mask × opacity × fill, so opacity and fill behave the same here. dissolve is the exception: alpha is used as the probability that a pixel is taken fully from the layer, using a fixed-seed random value per pixel. A missing mask counts as all white. With clip_to_below, the layer's mask is multiplied by the mask of the layer below; a layer below without a mask counts as white, so clipping changes nothing in that case. Layer images and masks are resized bilinearly to the background size. The hue, saturation, color and luminosity modes are computed in HSV, so they can differ slightly from Photoshop's versions. Source: nodes/layer_compositing.py and core/blend_modes.py.

docs.title: Layer Flatten
docs.text:
Merges all layers of a stack into a single image, like Layer → Flatten Image in Photoshop. Use it as the last step of a compositing chain.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → compositing → Compositing: Layer Flatten Good for Getting a normal image out of a layer stack so you can preview, save or keep editing

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: A layer stack is not an image yet. Until you flatten it, you cannot preview or save it. Layer Flatten renders the stack from the bottom layer up: each layer is mixed in using its blend mode, opacity, fill, mask and clipping.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Build a stack with Layer Stack Start and Layer Add.
  2. Connect the last LAYER_STACK to Layer Flatten → Preview Image or Save Image.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Setting Default What it does Tip stack — The layer stack to render. Connect the last node of your chain. Output Type Meaning IMAGE IMAGE The merged picture, values clamped to 0..1.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Flatten once, at the end. A flattened image no longer lets you adjust the individual layers.
  • You can flatten the same stack at two points (for example before and after one layer) to make a before/after comparison.
  • Run QA Image Diff on the original and the flattened image to see how much the composite changed.
Under the hood

Runs compose_stack from core/blend_modes.py. An empty stack raises an error. Source: nodes/layer_compositing.py.

docs.title: Layer Group
docs.text:
Takes a second layer stack, merges it into a single layer and adds that layer to your main stack. It works like a group folder in Photoshop that has its own blend mode, opacity and mask.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → compositing → Compositing: Layer Group (nest) Good for Keeping a set of grading layers together, fading a whole look in and out, masking several layers at once

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: When a look is made of several layers (for example a tint, a vignette and a glow), you often want to control them as one. Build those layers in their own stack, then nest the stack with Layer Group and set a single blend mode, opacity and mask for the whole thing.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Main chain: Load Image → Layer Stack Start → any Layer Add nodes → parent_stack.
  2. Group chain: a second Layer Stack Start with its own Layer Add nodes → sub_stack.
  3. Set group_blend_mode (try overlay) and group_opacity (try 0.8).
  4. Continue with more layers, or finish with Layer Flatten.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip parent_stack — The stack that receives the group. The group goes on top of it. sub_stack — The stack to merge into the group. Needs its own background layer from Layer Stack Start. group_blend_mode normal How the merged group mixes with the layers below. Same 27 modes as Layer Add. group_opacity 1.0 (0 to 1) How strongly the group shows. It is applied once, as the group's only strength control. Lower it to fade the whole look. group_mask (optional) none Where the group shows. White shows the group, black hides it.

Output: LAYER_STACK, the parent stack with the group on top.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• The merged group is a full-frame picture, including the background of its own stack. Use a blend mode such as overlay or soft_light, or a mask, so the layers below stay visible.
  • Put the mask on the group instead of on each layer inside it when you want one soft area for the whole look.
  • Build the group's layers on the same image as the main background if you want them to react to the same picture.
Under the hood

The sub-stack is rendered first with the same renderer as Layer Flatten (compose_stack in core/blend_modes.py), resized to the parent canvas, and appended to the parent stack as one ordinary layer that remembers its sub-stack. A group has no separate fill: group_opacity is the only strength control and is applied once (fixed in v1.5.4; earlier versions applied it twice, so the group looked weaker than the slider said). Source: nodes/layer_compositing.py.

docs.title: Layer Stack Start
docs.text:
Turns an ordinary image into the bottom layer of a layer stack, just like the Background layer in Photoshop. Every other compositing node builds on top of it.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → compositing → Compositing: Layer Stack Start Good for Starting any finishing composite: grading layers, light effects, texture overlays, nested groups

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
ComfyUI normally passes finished images between nodes. A layer stack is different: it keeps every layer separate (image, blend mode, opacity, mask) until you decide to merge them. That lets you rebuild the same stack as often as you like and change one layer without redoing the rest.

The stack travels on a special LAYER_STACK connection. Layer Stack Start creates it from your background image. You then add layers with Layer Add, optionally nest stacks with Layer Group, and turn the result back into a normal image with Layer Flatten.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Layer Stack Start (background).
  2. Connect its LAYER_STACK output to Layer Add.
  3. End the chain with Layer Flatten → Preview Image.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: Setting Default What it does Tip background — The image that becomes the bottom layer. Its size is the canvas size for the whole stack. Output Type Meaning LAYER_STACK LAYER_STACK A stack that contains only the background layer.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Feed in your final, full-size retouch as the background, so every layer you add is resized to match it.
  • Use a second Layer Stack Start when you want to build a group (for example a set of grading layers) separately, then nest it with Layer Group.
  • A LAYER_STACK cannot go into Preview Image or Save Image directly. Always finish with Layer Flatten.
Under the hood

The stack is a plain list of layer dictionaries. The background is stored as the first entry with blend mode normal, opacity 1, fill 1, no mask and no clipping. See nodes/layer_compositing.py for the wrapper and compose_stack in core/blend_modes.py for how a stack is rendered.

docs.title: Lens Distortion
docs.text:
Fixes the bending of straight lines caused by a lens (wide-angle barrel distortion, mild pincushion on short tele lenses), or does the reverse to give a clean image a lens look.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → geometry → Lens Distortion Corrector Good for Wide-angle portraits with stretched faces or curved edges, action-camera footage, creative lens effects

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Wide lenses bend straight lines near the frame edge and stretch faces. Correct this before face detection, alignment or geometry-sensitive edits so later steps work on a more natural shape.

Pick a preset that is close to your lens, or choose custom and enter the coefficients yourself. The presets are approximations, not profiles for a specific camera, so check the result by eye.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Lens Distortion Corrector → Preview Image.
  2. Choose a preset, for example canon_24mm_wide.
  3. Keep direction = inverse to correct the picture.
  4. Compare with the original and switch preset or use custom if lines still bend.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip preset no_op_identity canon_24mm_wide: barrel correction for wide lenses. sony_85mm_tele: mild pincushion correction. gopro_fisheye: strong barrel removal. no_op_identity: leaves the image unchanged. custom: use the five values below. When a preset is chosen, the five values below are ignored. direction inverse inverse corrects a distorted photo. forward adds distortion to a clean one. Use forward for creative effects. k1, k2, k3 0.0 (−1 to 1) Radial distortion: how much lines bend toward the edges. Used only with custom. Negative k1 corrects barrel distortion. p1, p2 0.0 (−0.1 to 0.1) Tangential distortion, for a lens that is slightly off-centre. Used only with custom. Rarely needed.

Output: image_rectified, the corrected (or distorted) picture (IMAGE).

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Correct lens distortion first, then crop, align and retouch.
  • Look at a straight edge near the corner of the frame to judge the result.
  • The output keeps the original frame size.
  • Run it before Face Detect Lite and Facial Aligner on wide portraits.
Under the hood

Implements the Brown-Conrady model with k1, k2, k3 (radial) and p1, p2 (tangential). The camera is assumed to have its focal length equal to the longer image side and its centre at the image centre, so values are approximate rather than calibrated. Preset values: canon_24mm_wide k1 −0.18, k2 0.08, k3 −0.02; sony_85mm_tele k1 0.03, k2 −0.01; gopro_fisheye k1 −0.35, k2 0.12, k3 −0.04; tangential terms are 0. Inverse mode uses Kornia undistort_image on GPU and OpenCV remap on CPU (and as a fallback); forward mode samples with grid_sample. Source: core/lens_distortion.py and nodes/lens_distortion_node.py.

docs.title: Lightroom Preset Contact Sheet
docs.text:
Lays out your photo with a whole collection of Lightroom presets applied, like a contact sheet: the original first, then one labelled tile per preset. A fast way to shortlist a look before you commit to one.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Color: Lightroom Preset Contact Sheet Good for Choosing a preset for a specific photo, reviewing a new preset pack, showing a client several looks at once, checking your favourites on a new shoot Speed 10 presets at 320 px in about 0.14 s on the GPU (after warm-up)

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Thumbnails in the Lightroom Preset browser are small. When you want to judge looks properly on your own image, this node renders the same presets at a size you choose and puts them in one image you can preview, save or send.

It uses the same preset folder, collections, favourites and recents as the Lightroom Preset node, and the same translation to ColorLab, so a tile here looks like the full node at strength 1.0.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Color: Lightroom Preset Contact Sheet → Preview Image on sheet.
  2. Pick a collection, for example a sub-folder of your presets or ★ Favorites.
  3. Run. Note the name of the look you like (the presets output lists them in order).
  4. Select that preset in a Lightroom Preset node to apply it at full size.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image — The photo to preview the presets on. Only the first frame of a batch is used. collection All Which presets to show: All, ★ Favorites, Recent, or one sub-folder of your preset folder. Favourites and recents are the ones you set in the Lightroom Preset browser. columns 4 Tiles per row (1 to 12). 4 to 6 suits a wide screen. thumb_size 320 Long edge of each tile in pixels (128 to 768). The photo is only scaled down, never up. 320 for a quick overview, 512 or more to judge skin tones. max_presets 24 Most presets to put on the sheet (1 to 200). Combine with search rather than rendering a huge sheet. search (optional) empty Only presets whose name contains every word you type. e.g. film warm. tone_engine (optional) local local uses edge-aware tone tools, closer to Lightroom; legacy uses ColorLab's simpler tone maths. Use the same engine as your Lightroom Preset node so the tiles match.

Outputs

Output What it is sheet One image with a labelled grid on a dark background: "Original" first, then each preset. A preset that is only partly supported has [!] after its name. presets The names of the presets on the sheet, one per line, in the same order as the tiles.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Star your best presets in the Lightroom Preset browser, then set collection to ★ Favorites to test them all on each new shoot.
  • A [!] tile is missing part of the original look (often a creative profile). Check that preset's report in the Lightroom Preset node before choosing it.
  • Use a photo with skin, neutrals and some saturated colour; presets that look similar on a landscape can differ a lot on skin.
  • Presets that cannot be read are left out of the sheet, so the presets list is the reliable record of what you see.
Under the hood

The first frame is downscaled once with area averaging so its long edge is at most thumb_size. Each preset is read and translated to ColorLab settings (parsed presets are cached by file and modification time), then applied with exposure in linear light, exactly as in the Lightroom Preset node at full strength. The local tone engine runs on the GPU when one is available. The tiles are assembled with Pillow: 6 px gaps, a label strip above each tile, names cut at 48 characters. Source: core/lr_preset_library.py.

docs.title: Lightroom Preset
docs.text:
Use the presets you already own from Lightroom Classic or Camera Raw on any image in ComfyUI. Pick a preset from a thumbnail grid, set the amount, and the node also tells you which settings it could and could not carry over.

The picture shows the original, the bundled Warm Film sample (.xmp) and the bundled Classic BW sample (.lrtemplate).

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Color: Lightroom Preset (XMP) Good for Reusing a Lightroom look on generated or edited images, keeping one grade across a batch, starting point for a ColorLab grade, browsing a large preset library visually Memory Peak VRAM 0.82 GB on the docs image

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A Lightroom preset is a list of slider values: Exposure +0.35, Highlights −45, a tone curve, some colour grading and so on. This node reads that list and recreates the look with the pack's own ColorLab engine, which has the same panels as Camera Raw. It is an approximation written for this pack, not Adobe's code, so judge the result by eye rather than expecting a pixel match.

Two file types are read:

  • .xmp: the modern preset format of Lightroom Classic and Camera Raw.
  • .lrtemplate: the older Lightroom preset format. It is read as plain data; no Lua code inside the file is ever run.

The node gives you three things: the graded image, the preset as ColorLab settings (params_json) that you can fine-tune or reuse, and a text report of what was applied.

docs.title: What is translated
docs.text:
Lightroom panel Carried over Basic Exposure, Contrast, Highlights, Shadows, Whites, Blacks (2012 process), Texture, Clarity, Dehaze, Vibrance, Saturation White balance Relative Temp / Tint. Absolute white balance (Kelvin, or Daylight, Cloudy, Shade, …) is converted relative to the photo's as-shot white. This is an approximation and is noted in the report. Tone curve Point curves (master, red, green, blue) and the parametric (region) curve HSL / Color Hue, saturation and luminance for all 8 colours Color Grading Shadows, midtones and highlights wheels with luminance, and Balance B&W Black-and-white conversion and the gray mixer, including magenta Calibration Red, green and blue primary hue and saturation, shadow tint Effects Grain, post-crop vignette

Exposure is applied in linear light, the way Lightroom does it.

docs.title: What is not possible
docs.text:
• Creative profiles such as Adobe's "Vintage 06" or "Artistic" looks. These are Adobe's own built-in colour tables and are not stored in the preset file. The Adobe Color and Adobe Standard profiles count as neutral and are fine.
  • Local masks (brush, gradients, subject or sky masks).
  • Lens corrections, sharpening and noise reduction. These are detail and optics settings rather than colour, so the report lists them separately.

Empty Point Color slots count as neutral. Everything the node skips is named in the report, never dropped silently.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Copy your presets into ComfyUI/models/lightroom_presets/. Sub-folders become collections.
  2. Load Image → Color: Lightroom Preset (XMP) → Preview Image. Connect report to a text display node.
  3. Click a thumbnail in the grid to choose a preset, then run the workflow.
  4. Lower strength if the look is too strong. Read the report to see what was not carried over.

No presets yet?

The pack ships two samples under PixelPro samples/: Warm Film.xmp and Classic BW.lrtemplate. They appear in the list straight away, so you can try the node before copying your own presets.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image — The picture to grade. preset first in list The preset to apply, from the preset folders. The browser grid sets this for you. Names include the sub-folder, e.g. PixelPro samples/Warm Film.xmp. strength 1.0 How much of the preset to apply (0 to 2), like Lightroom's preset Amount. 0 returns the original image. Slider amounts and curves scale with it; colour grading hues stay where they are. 0.5 to 0.8 often looks more natural on portraits. preset_path (optional) empty Full path to a preset file anywhere on disk. When filled, it overrides the list. Handy for a one-off file. It is not added to Recent. tone_engine (optional) local local uses edge-aware tone tools, closer to Lightroom. legacy uses ColorLab's original, simpler tone maths. Keep local unless you need to match an older ColorLab result. mask (optional) none Limits where the preset applies (white = full effect). Must match the image size. Use a subject or sky mask to grade only part of the frame.

Outputs

Output What it is image Your image with the preset applied. params_json The preset as ColorLab settings, already scaled by strength. Connect it to ColorLab to fine-tune the sliders, or to Apply ColorLab Preset to reuse the same look elsewhere. report Text listing the preset name, the settings applied, a "Not supported" list, a separate "Detail/optics, not colour" list (sharpening, noise, lens) and any notes, such as the white balance approximation.

docs.title: The preset browser
docs.text:
Under the preset dropdown the node shows a visual browser:

  • Collection: All, ★ Favorites, Recent, and one entry per sub-folder of your preset folder.
  • Search: shows only presets whose name contains every word you type.
  • Thumbnail grid: three rows of presets. Use ◀ ▶ to page through. The selected preset has a blue outline.
  • ☆ star (top right of a tile): click to add or remove a favourite.
  • Orange "!" badge (top left of a tile): the preset is only partly supported, for example it uses a creative profile or a local mask.
  • Footer: for the selected preset, lists what is not supported; otherwise shows how many presets match.
  • ⟳: reloads the preset list, so files you just copied in show up without restarting ComfyUI.
  • Hide grid / Show grid: folds the grid away to keep the node small.

Thumbnails show each preset on the image this node processed last. Before the first run they use a generated colour chart (grey ramp, skin, sky, foliage and primary patches). They are rendered on the CPU, about 10 ms each, so they do not compete with a running workflow for the GPU, and they are cached so a page renders only once.

Clicking a tile only changes the preset setting. Saved workflows and API prompts stay exactly the same as if you had picked the preset from the dropdown.

Note

The browser is drawn on the classic node canvas. With ComfyUI's newer Vue node interface turned on, it is not shown; the preset dropdown still works as usual.

docs.title: Managing a large library
docs.text:
• Folders are collections. Organise presets in sub-folders of ComfyUI/models/lightroom_presets/ the same way as your Lightroom preset groups (for example Portrait/, Film/, B&W/). Each sub-folder appears in the Collection list.
  • Favourites (★) and Recent (the last 12 presets you ran from the list) are saved in .jh_presets.json inside the preset folder. Every Lightroom Preset node and every workflow shares them, and copying the folder to another machine brings them along.
  • Search to narrow a collection quickly, e.g. warm film finds names containing both words.
  • Paging keeps the grid fast: only the visible page is rendered.
  • If you use extra_model_paths.yaml with a lightroom_presets entry, that folder is used instead.
  • To compare many presets on one photo at once, use the Lightroom Preset Contact Sheet.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Presets made for raw files often push Exposure, Shadows or Dehaze hard, because raw data has more headroom. On a JPEG or a generated image, start with strength around 0.6.
  • An absolute white balance (Kelvin) in a preset is only an estimate here; the report says so. If the colour looks off, remove the warmth in ColorLab with wb_temperature.
  • If a preset shows the orange "!", check the report. When the missing part is a creative profile, the look will be noticeably different from Lightroom.
  • Sharpening and noise reduction are never applied. Add Smart Sharpen after the grade if you need it.
  • To tweak a preset, send params_json into ColorLab and adjust from there instead of editing the .xmp file.
Under the hood

The .xmp file is parsed as an XMP packet and every crs: (camera-raw-settings) property is collected, from attributes or child elements. A .lrtemplate is tokenised as a Lua table literal and only the value.settings table is read; nothing is executed. Files over 4 MB are refused. Lightroom Classic still stores shadow and highlight colour-grading hue and saturation under the old SplitToning* keys, while ColorGrade* holds midtones and luminance; both are mapped. The parametric curve is rebuilt as a lookup table and combined with the master point curve. Absolute white balance is turned into a relative Temp shift from the mired difference between the target and the as-shot temperature. The resulting parameters run through the ColorLab pipeline with exposure in linear light. strength scales slider amounts and blends curves towards a straight line; colour-grading hues and switches are kept. The node re-runs automatically when the preset file changes on disk. Source: core/lr_preset.py, core/lr_preset_library.py.

docs.title: Look Select
docs.text:
Choose a complete look such as teal and orange, faded film or golden hour, and blend it in with one slider. Optionally keep skin tones out of the effect.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → looks → Look: Select Preset Good for Auditioning grades fast, a consistent style across a set, adding mood without building a colour chain

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Each look is a short recipe of colour moves: a shift of colour in the shadows or highlights (in LAB colour space), a gentle contrast curve, and saturation changes in selected hues. Look Select runs the recipe for you and blends the result with the original.

How it differs from LUT Preset: the LUT presets are fixed colour tables. Looks here are built from the pack's own colour tools, which lets them protect skin and treat colours selectively. Both are for quick results; for your own .cube files use LUT Import.

docs.title: The six looks
docs.text: Preset Character cinematic-teal-orange Classic cinema grade: teal shadows, orange highlights, mild S-curve. warm-skin-tone Portrait-safe warmth: lifts the orange band, calms greens, protects highlights. moody-green Deep editorial greens, crushed shadows, muted highlights. faded-film Lifted blacks, warm mids and gentle overall desaturation, like a soft film print. golden-hour Warm late-day cast, stronger orange and yellow, protected blues. desaturated-pop Muted background colour while orange-red skin tones stay lively.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect Load Image → Look: Select Preset → Preview Image.
  2. Pick a preset. Keep intensity at 0.7.
  3. Turn on protect_skin if faces start to look orange, green or washed out.
  4. To compare all six at once, open the six-look compare workflow below.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip preset cinematic-teal-orange The look to apply. See the table above. intensity 0.70 Mix between original (0) and full look (1). At 0 the image is returned unchanged. 0.4 to 0.7 for natural results; 1.0 for a stylised look. protect_skin off Reduces each step of the look on skin-coloured pixels. Try it with cinematic-teal-orange, golden-hour and moody-green.

Output: image — the graded image.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• warm-skin-tone and desaturated-pop are designed around skin. They are used with protect_skin on in the compare workflow, but the switch is not turned on automatically, so set it yourself.
  • Looks stack well with a final contrast tweak from Tone Curve.
  • For precise control over a single colour, switch to Hue/Saturation per Range and Saturation Mask.
  • To keep the same look across a series, fix preset and intensity and run the whole batch through the same node.
  • Skin protection is a colour-based guess. Warm wood or sand can also be protected. Check the result.
Under the hood

Presets are JSON files in the pack's presets/ folder with a list of operations; nodes/look_base.py runs them and blends with lerp(original, processed, intensity). The operations are a LAB colour shift (global, shadow, highlight and midtone weights), an RGB tone curve, a hue/saturation change inside a hue band, and a saturation change inside a saturation range. With protect_skin the skin mask (hue around 24° with a 28° band, multiplied by a saturation range of 0.18 to 0.95) scales down each step's change (the change is multiplied by one minus the mask). Output is clamped to [0, 1]. The dropdown is a fixed list in nodes/look_select.py, so adding a JSON file alone does not add a look. The protect_skin_default field in the JSON files is not read by the node.

docs.title: Luminosity Masking
docs.text:
Splits a picture into three soft masks by brightness (shadows, midtones, highlights), the same idea as luminosity masks in Photoshop, so you can grade or retouch just one tonal range.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Luminosity Masking Good for Dodge and burn, grading shadows and highlights separately, protecting the highlights, selective sharpening or denoising

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A luminosity mask selects pixels by how bright they are, not by where they are. That makes it a clean, edge-free selection: lift only the dark areas, cool only the highlights, or sharpen only the midtones, with no cutout to paint.

Here the three masks are soft and add up to 1 at every pixel, so shadows, midtones and highlights blend into each other without gaps or double coverage. You control where the bands change over (shadow_end, highlight_start) and how gradual the transition is (soft_edge).

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Luminosity Masking.
  2. Connect the mask_shadows output to Mask to Image → Preview Image to see the selection.
  3. Use the mask as the mask input of any other node, for example Tone Curve or Color Matcher, to limit its effect to the shadows.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image required The picture to analyse. luminance_source lab_l How brightness is measured. lab_l is perceptual (closest to what you see). ycbcr_y is fast and good for live previews. hsv_v is the simple maximum of R, G, B and less perceptual. lab_l for final work. shadow_end 0.33 (0 to 0.5) Brightness where the shadow band ends. Lower for only the deepest shadows. highlight_start 0.67 (0.5 to 1.0) Brightness where the highlight band begins. Must be above shadow_end. Raise for only specular highlights. soft_edge 0.1 (0.01 to 0.3) Width of the smooth transition at both edges. Small gives sharper bands, large gives gentler blends. 0.1 to 0.2 avoids banding in skin.

Outputs: mask_shadows, mask_midtones and mask_highlights, each a soft mask from 0 to 1.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• For dodge and burn, use mask_shadows to lift detail and mask_highlights to bring down blown areas.
  • Keep soft_edge generous (0.15 or more) when masks will gate strong edits, so no tonal boundary shows.
  • Narrow the midtone band (move shadow_end up and highlight_start down) to build a punchy "midtone only" mask for clarity or skin smoothing.
  • Combine two masks with Mask Combine (union, subtract, intersect and more) to make custom ranges such as "darks plus midtones".
  • On large images, ycbcr_y is far quicker than lab_l, so use it for interactive previews and switch to lab_l for the final run.
Under the hood

Brightness is computed in the chosen space: lab_l converts to linear RGB and uses the CIE L* (0 to 1), ycbcr_y the Kornia YCbCr Y channel, hsv_v the maximum channel. Shadows are 1 − smoothstep(shadow_end ± soft_edge/2), highlights are smoothstep(highlight_start ± soft_edge/2), and midtones are what remains (never below 0). The three are then divided by their sum, so they total 1 at every pixel. The code comments report roughly 120 ms for lab_l at 2K on CPU and roughly 7 ms for ycbcr_y at 1024 on CPU; treat these as indicative. shadow_end must be lower than highlight_start, and inputs outside 0..1 are clamped with a logged warning.

  • Tone Curve: apply a curve only to one range
  • ColorLab: global tone and colour; use the masks to restrict it
  • Frequency Separation: pair with a midtone mask for skin work

docs.title: LUT Export
docs.text:
Turns a colour grade built in ComfyUI into a portable .cube file. Take your look to other apps, or load it back with LUT Import.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → LUT Export (.cube) Good for Reusing a grade on many photos, sharing a look, matching video and stills

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text: You have a grade you like, built from several ComfyUI colour nodes. A LUT freezes that grade into one small file. You can then apply it quickly, over and over, or open it in other software.

docs.title: The LUT workflow
docs.text:
1. HALD Identity makes a neutral colour chart.
  2. Colour nodes grade the chart, for example Tone Curve. Use colour-only nodes: no blur, sharpen, resize or crop.
  3. LUT Export reads the graded chart and writes a .cube file to ComfyUI's output/ folder.
  4. Use the .cube file:
    • In ComfyUI with LUT Import, on any photo, optionally through a mask.
    • In other apps that read Adobe Cube 1.0 files. The project's release notes list DaVinci Resolve, Premiere Pro, OBS Studio and OCIO. Photoshop can load .cube files too, through a Color Lookup adjustment layer.

Check the file in your target app before relying on it. This pack writes and reads the standard format, and has no OCIO or Photoshop integration of its own.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Add HALD Identity (level 8).
  2. Connect its image to a colour node, such as Tone Curve, and set the grade.
  3. Add LUT Export. Connect the graded image to image and HALD Identity's level output to level.
  4. Set filename (for example my_look.cube) and title, then queue the prompt.
  5. Find the file in ComfyUI/output/. The node's path output shows where it was written.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image — The graded HALD chart. Must be the full chart, same size as it left HALD Identity. level 8 (range 2 to 16) HALD level of the chart. Must match HALD Identity; wire the two together. filename pack_lut.cube Output name. Relative names go to ComfyUI's output/ folder; absolute paths are used as given. .cube is added if missing. An existing file with the same name is overwritten. Pick a new name per look. title JHPixelPro LUT Name stored inside the file, shown by LUT browsers. Use a descriptive name such as Warm Portrait v2.

Output: path — the full path of the written .cube file.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Keep the chain colour-only. If the LUT looks wrong in another app, a spatial node (blur, sharpen, resize) between HALD and Export is the usual cause.
  • A LUT can only store colour changes that depend on each pixel's own colour. Local edits such as masks, dodge and burn, or skin smoothing cannot be baked in.
  • Level 8 is plenty for creative looks. Go higher only for very steep curves.
  • The output folder must exist. Missing parent folders for an absolute path raise an error.
  • Test the new file straight away: LUT Import on a photo, with strength 1.0.
Under the hood

The chart must be exactly L³ × L³ pixels for the given level and contain only finite values, otherwise the node raises an error. Values are clamped to [0, 1]. The file has the headers TITLE, LUT_3D_SIZE (L²), DOMAIN_MIN 0 0 0 and DOMAIN_MAX 1 1 1, followed by N³ lines (N = L²) of r g b with six decimals, red changing fastest, then green, then blue. Lines end with LF. Only the first image of a batch is exported. The write is plain file I/O, so there is nothing to speed up on a GPU.

docs.title: Related nodes
docs.text:
• HALD Identity — the neutral chart to start from.
  • LUT Import — apply the .cube back in ComfyUI.
  • Tone Match LUT — create a LUT from a reference photo in one step.
  • LUT Preset — bundled looks, no export needed.

docs.title: Example workflow
docs.text: LUT Export example workflow. HALD Identity makes a neutral chart, Tone Curve grades it, and LUT Export writes pixelpro_demo.cube to ComfyUI/output/; a Preview Any node shows the file path. No input image is needed. Open LUT Import to apply the file.

docs.title: LUT Import
docs.text:
Applies any Adobe Cube 1.0 .cube LUT to your photo. Use looks from other colourists, LUTs you exported from ComfyUI, or LUTs made in other apps.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → LUT Import (.cube) Good for Applying a favourite look, reusing a LUT from LUT Export, grading only part of a picture through a mask Speed About 0.5 s for a 2048 × 2048 image with a 65-point LUT on a CPU-only runner (from the project release notes). A GPU is faster.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A LUT (look-up table) is a saved colour grade in a small file. LUT Import reads that file and applies it to every pixel. Since it works on colour only, it is fast and gives the same result every time.

This node closes the loop of the LUT workflow: HALD Identity, grade, LUT Export, then LUT Import on any photo. It also loads .cube files that did not come from this pack.

For the six looks bundled with the pack, LUT Preset is quicker because it needs no file path.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Copy your .cube file into ComfyUI/input/.
  2. Connect Load Image → LUT Import (.cube) → Preview Image.
  3. Type the file name in filename, including .cube (for example my_look.cube).
  4. Set strength to 0.7 to 0.8 for a subtle dose, or 1.0 for the full look.

To grade only part of the picture, connect a MASK (for example from Saturation Mask) to the optional mask input.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip filename pack_lut.cube Path to the .cube file. A relative name is looked up in ComfyUI's input/ folder; an absolute path is used as written. The .cube extension is not added for you. Type the full file name. strength 1.00 Mix between original (0) and full LUT (1). 0.5 to 0.8 for a gentle creative look. mask (optional) none Limits the LUT to the white parts of the mask; grey parts get a partial effect. Feather the mask for smooth transitions.

Output: image — the graded image.

Where files are read from

LUT Export saves to ComfyUI/output/, but LUT Import reads relative names from ComfyUI/input/. Copy the file across, or give the full path.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Many creative LUTs are made for a specific colour space (for example log video). On a normal sRGB photo they can look flat or too strong. Lower strength or try a different LUT.
  • Do skin retouching first, then the look. A strong LUT can exaggerate blotchy skin.
  • Use mask to keep the LUT off skin or off a logo. Build the selection with Saturation Mask or Luminosity Masking.
  • Only 3D LUTs are supported (files with LUT_3D_SIZE). One-dimensional LUTs are rejected.
Under the hood

The file is parsed for TITLE, LUT_3D_SIZE (2 to 256), DOMAIN_MIN and DOMAIN_MAX; the body must contain exactly size³ lines of three numbers, or the node raises an error. The image is clamped to the domain, normalised, and sampled with trilinear interpolation via grid_sample (border padding, no extrapolation). The result is blended as in * (1 - s) + lut(in) * s, where s is strength multiplied by the mask. Masks can be (B, H, W) or (B, 1, H, W). Tetrahedral interpolation is not implemented. The image must be RGB with three channels; alpha is not supported.

docs.title: Example workflow
docs.text: LUT Import example workflow. The workflow builds its own LUT (HALD Identity → Tone Curve → LUT Export) and wires the file path into LUT Import, so it runs without any extra file. For your own LUT, type its file name (relative names are read from ComfyUI/input/) or an absolute path. Copy workflows/sample_portrait.jpg into ComfyUI/input/.

docs.title: LUT Preset
docs.text:
Pick a ready-made colour grade from a dropdown and dial it in. The looks are bundled .cube LUTs, so there is no file to find or load.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Color: LUT Preset Good for Quickly auditioning a look, a starting point for a grade, applying a consistent tone to a batch

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A LUT (look-up table) is a saved colour grade: for every input colour it stores the output colour. Colourists use LUTs to carry one look across many shots and apps.

This node is the quick route. It ships six generic looks and applies them with the same engine as LUT Import. Use LUT Import instead when you have your own .cube file.

See the LUT Preset gallery for before and after pictures of every preset.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect Load Image → Color: LUT Preset → Preview Image.
  2. Choose a preset. Start with warm-portrait or cinematic-teal-orange.
  3. Lower intensity to 0.6 to 0.85 if the full look is too strong.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip preset neutral-identity The bundled look to apply (list below). neutral-identity changes nothing; use it to check your wiring. intensity 1.00 Mix between original (0) and full look (1). 0.6 to 0.85 is a natural dose for portraits. Preset Character neutral-identity No change; a baseline for comparison. warm-portrait Warmer, softer portrait direction. cool-portrait Cleaner, cooler cast. cinematic-teal-orange Cool shadows, warm highlights and skin tones. soft-pastel Lighter, lower-contrast colour. high-contrast Punchier separation.

Output: image — the graded image.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Grade after retouching. Skin work and frequency separation behave best on the neutral file.
  • Use intensity as your strength control. A look at 0.7 often reads more natural than at 1.0.
  • If a look pushes skin too far, try Look Select, which has a protect_skin switch.
  • Make your own look with the LUT workflow and bring it back with LUT Import.
Under the hood

The dropdown lists every .cube file in the pack's presets/ folder, so the list follows that folder. Each file is parsed as Adobe Cube 1.0 (all bundled files are 17-point cubes) and applied with trilinear interpolation through grid_sample, honouring any DOMAIN_MIN / DOMAIN_MAX header. intensity is a linear blend original * (1 - s) + lut * s. Colours outside the LUT domain are clamped to its edge, not extrapolated.

docs.title: Mask Cleanup
docs.text:
The first stop for a mask from SAM, rembg or any other cutout tool. It deletes stray specks, fills small holes inside the subject, and can finish with an even feather.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → mask → Mask: Cleanup Good for Removing floating dots, filling pin-holes in a subject, producing a clean evenly feathered mask

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
AI segmentation often leaves two kinds of mess: tiny floating islands of selection in the background, and small holes inside the subject. Both come from the mask being a set of connected pixel groups. This node finds each group and decides by its size in pixels whether to keep it, instead of by a brush radius. That makes it more predictable than erode-and-dilate for tidying up.

The mask is first turned into pure black and white at the threshold. Then islands smaller than min_island_area are removed, and holes smaller than max_hole_area are filled. A hole that touches the image border is never filled, because it is really background.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect the mask from your segmentation node.
  2. Keep the defaults (island 64, hole 64, no feather). Raise the areas for bigger images.
  3. Add feather_px 3 to 6 if you want a soft edge.
  4. Compare before and after with Mask Preview.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip threshold 0.5 Pixels above this value count as subject. Lower it to include faint areas. min_island_area 64 Delete subject blobs smaller than this many pixels. 0 = off. Scale with image size. Try 200 to 2000 on a 2 K photo. max_hole_area 64 Fill enclosed holes smaller than this many pixels. 0 = off. Never fills background that touches the image border. feather_px 0.0 Soft-edge distance, measured from the cleaned edge. 0 = hard black and white. 0 to 256. The full soft ramp spans twice this value. connectivity 8 8 treats diagonal pixels as connected; 4 only counts side neighbours. Leave on 8 for most masks.

Output: mask (MASK).

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Use it first in a mask chain, then Edge-Aware Mask Refiner or Sub-Pixel Mask Refiner.
  • Its feather is an even distance from the edge, so the half-way line stays on the original outline. A blur would shrink thin parts of the subject instead.
  • If a real part of the subject disappears (a small earring, a button), min_island_area is too high.
  • If a real hole disappears (a gap between an arm and the body), lower max_hole_area.
Under the hood

The mask is binarised with mask > threshold. Components are labelled with cv2.connectedComponentsWithStats. Holes are found on the inverted mask using the complementary connectivity (8 for the subject pairs with 4 for the holes), which is the standard pairing that stops a hole from leaking diagonally. The feather is alpha = clip(0.5 + sd / (2 * feather_px), 0, 1), where sd is the signed distance to the boundary from cv2.distanceTransform (positive inside). It runs on the CPU, one batch item at a time. Source: core/mask_cleanup.py.

docs.title: Mask Combine
docs.text:
Combine two masks into one: add them, cut one out of the other, keep only where they overlap, and more. Optionally feather both before combining.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → mask → Mask: Combine Good for Adding a hand-painted area to an automatic mask, cutting eyes out of a skin mask, keeping the overlap of two selections

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
This is the mask version of Photoshop's selection modes: add to selection, subtract from selection, intersect with selection. mask_a is your base mask and mask_b is the one you apply to it.

Operation Result Think of it as union Larger of the two values at each pixel Add to selection (keeps soft edges) add a + b, clamped to 0..1 Add, with overlaps brightening subtract a - b, clamped Subtract B from A difference a * (1 - b) Cut B out of A, with soft edges respected intersect Smaller of the two values Only where both overlap multiply a * b Overlap, with soft values blended xor Where only one of them is set Everything except the overlap

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect your main mask to mask_a and the second mask to mask_b.
  2. Choose operation. For "cut the eyes out of the skin mask", use difference with the eyes as mask_b.
  3. Leave blend_mode on hard unless the edges need softening.
  4. Check the result with Mask Preview.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip operation union How the two masks are combined. See the table above. blend_mode hard hard uses the masks as they are. soft_feather blurs both masks first. Use soft_feather for a smooth blend between regions. opacity 1.0 Strength of the operation. 0 returns mask_a unchanged; 1 gives the full result. 0 to 1. Lower it for a subtle edit. feather_sigma 0.0 Blur strength (pixels) used by soft_feather. 0 to 64. Has no effect in hard mode.

Output: mask (MASK).

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Order matters for subtract and difference: mask_b is removed from mask_a.
  • Both masks must have the same width and height. One of them can be a single-frame mask used for a whole batch.
  • To soften only the result, combine with hard, then feather with Mask Edge Smoother.
  • Combine a Luminosity Masking mask with a subject mask using multiply or intersect to adjust only the highlights on the subject.
Under the hood

Inputs are clamped to 0..1. In soft_feather mode both masks get a Gaussian blur (kernel = 2 * round(3 * sigma) + 1, replicate padding). The operation runs on the (possibly blurred) masks and is clamped; the final result is a * (1 - opacity) + combined * opacity. A batch of 1 is broadcast against a larger batch. Source: core/mask_combine.py.

docs.text:

  • Mask Edge Smoother to soften the result

docs.title: Example workflow
docs.text: Mask Combine example workflow. Copy workflows/sample_portrait.jpg and workflows/sample_binary_mask.png into ComfyUI/input/. It intersects the subject mask with the Luminosity Masking highlights, with soft_feather on the edge, so only the bright parts of the subject stay selected. It uses only core ComfyUI nodes and this pack.

docs.title: Mask Edge Smoother
docs.text:
Removes stair-steps and wobble from a mask edge without turning the whole mask into a blur. With a guide image, the smoothing respects the real edges in your photo.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → mask → Mask: Edge Smoother Good for Cleaning jagged AI-segmentation outlines, smoothing a mask after morphology, keeping edges tied to the photo

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A normal blur treats every pixel the same, so it also rounds off real corners. A bilateral filter averages a pixel only with neighbours that have a similar value. In a mask, that means the smoothing happens along an edge but not across it. The result: a cleaner, smoother outline that does not melt.

If you also give it a guide photo, it compares photo colours instead of mask values. Smoothing then follows the real boundary in the image, so the mask hugs the subject.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect the mask. Optionally connect the same photo to guide.
  2. Start with sigma_spatial 4, sigma_range 0.1, iterations 1.
  3. If the edge is still jagged, raise iterations to 2 or 3.
  4. Choose backend gpu on a CUDA machine for large images.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip sigma_spatial 4.0 How far (in pixels) the smoothing reaches. 0.1 to 64. Larger = smoother, slower. sigma_range 0.1 How different two values can be and still be averaged together. 0.001 to 1. Low keeps edges sharp; high smooths more. iterations 1 Number of smoothing passes. 1 to 5. guide (optional) none A photo that steers the smoothing. Must match the mask in size. Use the original photo. backend opencv opencv runs on the CPU. gpu runs in PyTorch on CUDA and always uses the guide. See the note below.

Output: mask (MASK).

Guide and backend

The opencv backend only uses the guide if the optional opencv-contrib package is installed. Otherwise it quietly falls back to a plain bilateral filter. The gpu backend always honours the guide. If no CUDA device is available, gpu runs on the CPU and logs a warning that it will be slow.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Run it after Mask Morphology or Mask Combine, which can leave small jaggies.
  • For a soft transparent edge (a feather), follow with Sub-Pixel Mask Refiner. This node smooths a shape; it does not build a feather band.
  • A very large sigma_spatial is slow. Prefer a few small passes over one huge one.
Under the hood

The filter diameter is max(3, 2 * round(sigma_spatial) + 1). The opencv path uses cv2.ximgproc.jointBilateralFilter when a guide is given and the contrib module exists, otherwise cv2.bilateralFilter. The gpu path is a pure-PyTorch shift-and-accumulate bilateral pass (L1 colour distance, reflect-101 borders), so memory grows with image size, not with the kernel area. Source: core/mask_edge_smooth.py.

docs.text:

docs.text: Mask Edge Smoother example workflow. Copy workflows/sample_portrait.jpg and workflows/sample_binary_mask.png into ComfyUI/input/. It uses backend = gpu (needs an NVIDIA GPU) with the portrait as the guide to smooth stair-stepped mask edges. With the default opencv backend the node runs on the CPU. It uses only core ComfyUI nodes and this pack.

docs.title: Mask Morphology
docs.text:
Grow a mask, shrink it, fill small gaps, remove thin spurs, or extract just its outline. It is the mask version of Photoshop's Select → Modify → Expand / Contract.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → mask → Mask: Morphology Good for Expanding a mask to cover halos, contracting to remove a fringe, closing small holes, making an edge band

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Morphology changes the shape of a mask rather than its softness. The idea is to slide a small round "brush" (the kernel) across the mask edge. Seven operations are available:

Operation What happens Typical use dilate Mask grows outward Cover a halo; make room for a feather erode Mask shrinks inward Remove a coloured fringe at the edge open Erode, then dilate Delete small white specks and thin spurs close Dilate, then erode Fill small black holes and gaps gradient Dilated minus eroded An outline band around the edge tophat Original minus open Keeps only the small bright bits that open would remove blackhat close minus original Keeps only the small dark gaps that close would fill

For removing specks or holes by their size (rather than by brush radius), Mask Cleanup is easier to control.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect any mask to Mask Morphology.
  2. Pick erode with radius 3 to shrink the selection and trim an edge fringe, or dilate to expand it.
  3. Preview with Mask Preview.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip operation dilate Which of the seven operations to run. See the table above. radius 3 Radius of the round kernel, in pixels. 1 to 64. Roughly how many pixels the edge moves. iterations 1 How many times to repeat the operation. 1 to 10. For big changes, a larger radius is usually cleaner than many iterations.

Output: mask (MASK).

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• To make a feathered ring around the edge, run gradient, then soften it with Mask Edge Smoother or Sub-Pixel Mask Refiner.
  • After dilate or erode, the edge can look jagged. Finish with a feather.
  • Use close before building a Trimap if your mask has pin-holes.
  • Morphology also works on soft masks: it grows and shrinks the grey values (a grayscale dilate takes the local maximum).
Under the hood

An elliptical structuring element of size 2 * radius + 1 is built with cv2.getStructuringElement. dilate and erode call cv2.dilate and cv2.erode; the other operations use cv2.morphologyEx. It runs on the CPU in float32, one batch item at a time, and the result goes back to the input device. Source: core/mask_morphology.py. For very large radii on the GPU, avoid kornia.morphology; it uses a lot of memory.

docs.text:

docs.title: Example workflow
docs.text: Mask Morphology example workflow. Copy workflows/sample_portrait.jpg and workflows/sample_binary_mask.png into ComfyUI/input/. It runs close at radius 64 to seal the small shadow gap by the nose without growing the outline. It uses only core ComfyUI nodes and this pack.

docs.title: Mask Preview
docs.text:
See what a mask really does. It turns a mask into a picture you can look at, like Photoshop's quick-mask overlay or the "show mask" view.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → mask → Mask: Preview Overlay Good for Checking a mask's coverage, spotting holes and halos, judging soft edges, previewing a cutout on a checkerboard

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A raw mask is a grey image that is hard to judge. Four views make it clear:

Mode What you see Best for overlay Photo tinted with a colour where the mask is on Checking coverage heatmap Mask values as a colour map (0 = cold, 1 = hot) Finding soft or partial values mask_only The mask as grey-scale The plain view cutout Photo shown only where the mask is on, over a checkerboard Judging the cutout, like a transparent layer

The preview is for looking only. Do not feed its output back as a mask. Connect it to a Preview Image node.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect the mask to mask and your photo to the optional image.
  2. Choose overlay with opacity 0.5 and show_edges on.
  3. Connect preview to a Preview Image node.
  4. Switch to cutout to see how it would look on a transparent background.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip mode overlay Which of the four views to draw. See the table above. color red Tint colour for overlay, and the colour of the edge line. Pick a colour that contrasts with the photo. Eight colours are available, from red to white and black. opacity 0.5 Strength of the tint (overlay) or the heatmap blend. 0 to 1. colormap turbo The colour scale used by heatmap. Names come from Kornia's colormap list, such as turbo, viridis, jet. show_edges off Draws the 0.5 contour of the mask as a thin line in color. Handy for judging how tight the edge is. image (optional) none The background photo. Without it you get a neutral grey background (a bare colour map in heatmap mode). A 4-channel image is accepted; the alpha channel is ignored.

Output: preview (IMAGE).

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Use heatmap on a feathered mask to see exactly how wide the soft band is.
  • Use cutout with a contrasting checkerboard to find halos that a flat background would hide.
  • Use show_edges in overlay mode to compare two masks. Run the node twice with different colours.
  • The image and the mask must have the same width and height.
Under the hood

overlay mixes the photo toward the colour by opacity * mask. heatmap uses kornia.color.apply_colormap with the chosen colormap and blends it with the photo by opacity. cutout mixes the photo and an 8 px checkerboard by the mask. The edge line is a one-pixel band, built from dilation minus erosion of the mask thresholded at 0.5. Source: core/mask_preview.py.

docs.text:

  • Alpha Matte for soft cutouts to view in cutout mode
  • Trimap Builder, whose three zones show clearly in heatmap
  • QA Image Diff for comparing two images instead

docs.title: Motion / Zoom Blur
docs.text:
Fakes a moving camera or a zoom during the exposure. Blur only the background for a panning look, or streak the frame toward a centre point.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → filters → Filters: Motion / Zoom Blur Good for Panning shots, speed effects, zoom bursts, adding energy to a static background Speed At 4K on a GPU: motion 200 px about 1.4 s, zoom about 0.1 s, under 1 GB VRAM.

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
• motion averages the picture along a straight line, like a camera or subject moving during the exposure. Set the direction with angle and the length with distance.
  • zoom averages along the rays toward a centre point, like turning the zoom ring during the exposure. Pixels near the centre barely change; the frame edge streaks the most.

For a panning look, blur the background only. Connect an inverted subject mask to mask: the blur applies where the mask is white.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Filters: Motion / Zoom Blur → Preview Image.
  2. Motion: set mode to motion, angle 0 for a sideways streak, and try distance 60.
  3. Zoom: set mode to zoom and keep zoom at 0.15, with the centre at 0.5 / 0.5.
  4. Optional: connect an inverted subject mask to mask to keep the subject sharp.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip mode motion motion = blur in one direction. zoom = streaks toward a centre point. angle 0 -180 to 180 degrees. 0 = horizontal, 90 = vertical. Used by motion only. Match the direction the subject moves. distance 20 0 to 1000 pixels. Blur length for motion. Scale it with image size: 60 px at 2K is subtle, 200 px at 4K is strong. zoom 0.15 0 to 0.9. The frame edge streaks over this fraction of its distance to the centre. Used by zoom only. 0.1 to 0.3 looks natural. center_x, center_y 0.5, 0.5 0 to 1. Where the zoom streaks point to, across and down the frame. Used by zoom only. Put it on the subject's face or eye. mask (optional) none Blur only where the mask is white; elsewhere the image is unchanged. Use an inverted subject mask.

Output

Output What it is image The blurred image, same size as the input. motion with distance under 0.5, or zoom of 0, returns the input unchanged.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Pass the subject mask through Mask Combine (invert) and soften its edge with Mask Edge Smoother so the sharp subject does not show a hard rim.
  • Blur first, then add Smart Sharpen to the subject only.
  • Very long distance on a busy background becomes a smear. Raise it gradually.
  • Move center_x and center_y onto the subject for a zoom burst that pulls the eye in.
Under the hood

Both modes are a box blur along a one-dimensional path. A box of n1 × n2 taps is the same as a box of n1 taps at spacing 1 followed by one of n2 taps at spacing n1, so a blur D pixels long needs about 2·√D warps instead of D. Zoom uses the same trick in log-radius, where scalings add up. Each warp is a bilinear grid_sample with reflection at the borders, and the average keeps the overall brightness. Memory stays proportional to the number of pixels. ComfyUI hands images over on the CPU; the node moves the work to the GPU when one exists and falls back to the CPU on out-of-memory. The optional mask blends the result with the original. Source: core/directional_blur.py.

docs.title: Palette Extract
docs.text:
Pulls the dominant colours out of an image, the way you would pick swatches with the eyedropper. You get a swatch strip, the colour codes as text, and a posterized copy of the picture.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → color → Color: Palette Extract Good for Building a colour palette from a reference photo, checking a colour grade, a flat-colour (posterize) look, feeding hex codes to other tools

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Use it when you want to know "what colours is this picture really made of?". It groups similar pixels together using CIE LAB, a colour space built around how the eye sees differences, so the groups match what you would call "one colour". Dark and bright versions of a similar hue stay separate when they look different.

Colours are sorted by share, biggest first. The share tells you how much of the picture (or of the masked area) each colour covers.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Load Image → Color: Palette Extract → Preview Image on the palette output.
  2. Set colors to 5 or 6 to start.
  3. Optional: connect a subject mask to mask so the background does not take over the palette.
  4. Send palette_json to a text display or save node to keep the hex codes.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip colors 6 How many colours to find (2 to 16). 4 to 8 reads well for portraits. More colours means finer shades. mask (optional) none Only pixels inside the mask (value above 0.5) count towards the palette and the shares. Use a subject or skin mask. If one image in a batch has an empty mask, that image uses its whole frame (a warning is logged) instead of failing the batch.

Outputs

Output What it is palette A 1024 × 192 swatch strip with one equal-width band per colour, biggest share on the left. palette_json Text list like [{"hex": "#c8a58b", "rgb": [200, 165, 139], "share": 0.31}, …], largest share first. With a batch of one image this is a flat list; with a batch of several images it is a list of lists, one per image. quantized Your image with every pixel replaced by its nearest palette colour (a posterized, flat-colour look). It always covers the whole frame, even when a mask is used.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Use colors 2 or 3 to see the main colour split of a grade, such as warm skin versus cool shadows.
  • Mask the subject first, otherwise a big sky or backdrop uses up most of the colours.
  • The result is the same every time for the same image and settings.
  • Compare two versions of an edit by extracting palettes from both and comparing the hex codes.
  • Chain quantized into Color Matcher or view it next to the original for a quick look at the tonal structure.
Under the hood

The image is converted to CIE LAB (Kornia). K-means++ seeding and 25 Lloyd iterations run on a random subsample of at most 200,000 pixels (fixed seed 0, so results repeat). Then every pixel (or every masked pixel for the shares) is assigned to its nearest centre in chunks of about one million pixels, so memory stays small. Centres are converted back to sRGB and rounded to 8 bits; the same rounded values drive the strip, the JSON and quantized. If the image has fewer distinct colours than colors, the extra entries have a share of 0. Source: core/palette.py.

docs.text:

  • Skin Tone Tri-Region for per-region skin tone work
  • Mask Combine to build the subject mask

docs.title: Example workflow

docs.title: Pyramid Blend
docs.text:
Composites one image over another through a mask and hides the seam. Fine detail switches over sharply while colour and exposure fade over a wide area, so you do not see a hard edge or a brightness step.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → compositing → Compositing: Pyramid Blend Good for Pasting a graded or retouched face back into a photo, object and face swaps, stitching two exposures

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
A plain mask composite shows its edge whenever the two images differ in brightness or colour. This node splits both images into detail bands (a Laplacian pyramid, the classic Burt-Adelson method) and blends each band separately: fine bands use a narrow transition, coarse bands a wide one. The seam blends in without ghosting.

Choose it over Layer Add with a mask when the two images do not match perfectly at the edge.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Put the base photo in image_a and the edited version (or the other photo) in image_b. They must have the same size.
  2. Connect a MASK to mask: white takes image_b, black keeps image_a.
  3. Leave levels at 5, then raise it if a seam is still visible.
  4. Preview Image.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip image_a — Base image, kept where the mask is 0. image_b — Overlay image, taken where the mask is 1. mask — Where image_b replaces image_a. A hard mask is fine; the pyramid does the feathering. levels 5 (1 to 10) Pyramid depth. More levels give a wider, smoother transition. 1 is a plain alpha composite. Try 4 to 6 first.

Output: image, the blended picture (IMAGE).

All three inputs must share the same height and width. A batch of 1 on any input is reused for the others.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• Use fewer levels (1 to 3) for a tight edge, more (7 to 10) to hide big exposure or colour differences.
  • If you see colour halos around the seam, lower levels.
  • Make the mask first with Mask Cleanup or Edge-Aware Mask Refiner for a clean cut-out shape.
  • Grade the face with a LUT first (LUT Preset), then blend it back through a face mask.
Under the hood

Both images get a Laplacian pyramid (band-pass layers plus a low-pass residual) and the mask gets a Gaussian pyramid, built with Kornia pyrdown / pyrup. Each band is blended as band_a × (1 − mask) + band_b × mask, then the pyramid is collapsed. Images are replicate-padded to a multiple of 2 ** (levels - 1) and cropped back, so any size works. The depth is lowered automatically so the smallest level stays at least 8 px on its short side. Identical inputs, an all-0 mask or an all-1 mask return the source unchanged. Source: core/pyramid_blend.py.

docs.title: QA Image Diff
docs.text:
Put your before and after side by side for the computer. It draws a map of what changed and gives you numbers, so you can check that a retouch only touched what you meant it to.

In ComfyUI Add Node → ComfyUI-JH-PixelPro → qa → QA: Image Diff (SSIM/PSNR) Good for Checking where a retouch changed pixels, comparing two settings or pipelines, verifying an edit stayed inside a mask

docs.title: When to use it
docs.text:
Our eyes miss subtle changes. This node measures them:

  • Diff image: shows where the two images differ. Bright means a bigger change.
  • SSIM (structural similarity): from about 0 to 1. 1 means identical structure. It reacts to changes in texture and edges more than to a small overall brightness shift.
  • PSNR (in dB): higher means closer. Identical images give the cap, 100 dB.
  • Report: JSON with ssim, psnr, mae (average absolute difference, 0 to 1), max_abs (largest single difference) and changed_pct (percentage of pixels that moved by more than 1/255).

Use it to prove that a frequency-separation or smoothing pass left the eyes and hair untouched, or to see exactly which areas a new setting changes.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text:
1. Connect the original to image_a and the retouched version to image_b. Both must have the same width and height.
  2. Leave diff_mode on heatmap and amplify on 4.
  3. Connect diff to a Preview Image node. Connect report to a text preview node to read the numbers.
  4. Optionally connect a mask to measure only one area.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Setting Default What it does Tip diff_mode heatmap heatmap is a colour map of the strongest channel difference. abs is the per-channel absolute difference. ssim_map shows where the structure changed (bright = changed). Start with heatmap. amplify 4.0 Gain applied to the difference so small changes show up. Not used by ssim_map. 1 to 100. Raise it to reveal subtle edits. window_size 11 Size of the SSIM window (odd number). Larger = judges coarser structure. 3 to 31. Reduced automatically on small images. mask (optional) none Restricts all the numbers to this region, weighted by the mask. The diff picture itself is not masked.

Outputs: diff (IMAGE), ssim (FLOAT), psnr (FLOAT), report (STRING).

Batches

The ssim and psnr outputs refer to the first image of a batch only. The report lists every item.

docs.title: Tips from retouching
docs.text:
• A very high amplify makes tiny rounding differences light up. Compare against the numbers, not only the picture.
  • Compare against the mask you used for the edit. If changed_pct inside the mask is high but outside is near zero, the edit stayed in place.
  • If the mask is entirely black, the numbers return neutral values (SSIM 1, PSNR 100, others 0).
  • Use ssim_map to ignore uniform brightness shifts and spot only structural changes.
Under the hood

SSIM is computed with kornia.metrics.ssim over the chosen window and averaged over channels. PSNR is -10 log10(MSE), capped at 100 dB. heatmap applies the Kornia turbo colormap to the maximum channel difference times amplify. With a mask, every metric becomes a mask-weighted mean. Images must match in size (there is no automatic resize); a batch of 1 is broadcast. Source: core/qa_diff.py.
